又看到一个很有前景的项目 @omenapp 
至少我认为是这样

最近链上期权赛道的热度明显回来了。
比如 $DRV 从 8 月至今已经涨了约 5 倍，价格和 TVL 都创下新高。
而 Omen 的方向，简单说是一个面向散户的碎片化期权交易所。

1/ 核心创新在于碎片化期权
传统美股期权通常是1 张合约 = 100 股，参与门槛很高，很多策略动辄需要几千甚至几万美元。
而 Omen 设想的期权合约采用 1x multiplier：1 张合约 = 1 股。
这样一来，用户就可以用几美元、几十美元去表达自己的交易观点。

2/ 除了合约单位更小，Omen 还强调几个方向
链抽象。区块链只作为后台结算层，尽量不让用户感知复杂链上操作。
24/7 期权交易。让期权像加密市场一样全天候交易。
期权与永续交叉保证金。让期权和永续不再是割裂的产品，而是在同一保证金体系下互补。

3/ 团队与资方
创始人 @djeong 的背景也比较匹配这个方向。
他早期曾是 Apple 校园领袖，之后做过 DoorDash 软件工程师，也曾在全球知名的量化交易公司 SIG 担任量化交易员。兼具技术和量化交易背景。
官网信息显示，Omen 已获得美国风投机构 Susa Ventures 投资。Susa 不是 crypto-native 基金，但其代表案例包括 Robinhood，在散户金融产品和早期 fintech 判断上有一定参考价值。

整体来看，Omen 不是单纯的链上期权叙事，而是尝试把传统期权产品重新设计成更适合散户的形态，更小单位、更低门槛、更连续交易体验，以及更好的保证金效率。
当然，期权交易所最终能不能跑出来，核心还是要看流动性和真实用户需求。

quoted_text:
Seven days ago, we started an experiment in Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI).

We wanted to explore a simple question: What happens when we let an AI agent iteratively improve its own harness?

So we let Lobe Agent run for an entire week, using our RSI framework to explore and optimize its own harness.

Today, we're sharing the results.

We evaluated the resulting system on FrontierHarness, using Kimi K3 as the underlying model.

Key results:

• 70.0% pass rate (21/30), ranking #1 among 13 harnesses in our preliminary comparison.

• $1.68 per successful task, compared to $3.47 for Codex and $18.34 for Claude Code.

• 86.2% median cache hit rate, with a median completion time of 7m 19s on successful tasks.

These preliminary results suggest that harness-level optimization may be a promising path toward improving agent performance and efficiency without modifying the underlying model weights.

The comparison includes selected retries and differences in execution environments, and should not be interpreted as an official leaderboard ranking.

We plan to fully open-source the experiment's scripts, execution trajectories, and a detailed technical report to enable reproducibility and further investigation.

Alongside this experiment, we've also been building Awesome-RSI, an open-source research map of Recursive Self-Improvement.

The repository brings together papers, frameworks, benchmarks, and open-source projects spanning model-level and harness-level self-improvement, automated AI research, and safety.

It has already accumulated 80+ commits, and we're continuously expanding and refining the collection.

https://t.co/2ToHszAi9G

We believe open research, reproducible experiments, and community collaboration are essential to advancing this field.

We welcome researchers and developers to contribute, share their work, and explore RSI together. ❤️

quoted_text:
There’s currently some FUD about @Backpack, subtly implying that the exchange is still young (only 4 years old) and that withdrawing $10K gets delayed for 4 hours.

I want to clarify: This is an optional security feature, not a bug or “stuck funds.”

Backpack has a Withdrawal Delay feature:
Go to Settings → Accounts: Exchange → Security → Withdrawal Delay. 

Users can turn it on themselves and choose the waiting time (e.g. 4h, 12h, 24h, etc.).

It only applies when withdrawing to a new external wallet address (not yet saved in the Address Book, or saved for less time than the delay you’ve set).

Addresses that have been whitelisted / saved longer than the delay period are withdrawn normally and quickly.

Internal transfers between sub-accounts are not affected by the delay.

Armani even actively recommends using this feature, going as far as saying that “instant withdrawals are an utterly stupid thing that crypto has normalized,” because it helps protect against hacks, clipboard malware, mistyped addresses, etc.

A guy who left over $4M on the Fomo app got hacked. Today, $80M stored on Ledger was completely drained due to a supply chain issue.

Yet when Backpack is trying to protect its users, some people use that as a reason to criticize it?

text:
robinhood:0xbc2283d12b1f2f46c1613ae672e95c55b69ca414 和 $PAPER 到底啥关系， 以及 @papertrade_xyz 值不值得冲？

首先 robinhood:0xbc2283d12b1f2f46c1613ae672e95c55b69ca414 是 PaperDAO 的代币，而 $paper 是 Papertrade 的代币。

持有 robinhood:0xbc2283d12b1f2f46c1613ae672e95c55b69ca414，意味着间接持有 PaperDAO 金库的相应份额。DAO 募集资金参与 Papertrade，将获得的 $PAPER 再分配给 robinhood:0xbc2283d12b1f2f46c1613ae672e95c55b69ca414 持有者。

说白了 robinhood:0xbc2283d12b1f2f46c1613ae672e95c55b69ca414 的价值非常依赖 $PAPER 的表现，而且这中间还隔了一层 DAO 的运营和治理，以及金库净值，赎回机制都是未知数。真要是看好 Paperstrade 这个 Hyperliquid 生态的链上合成永续合约协议，不如直接买 $PAPER 来的直接。

至于 @papertrade_xyz 值不值得冲？先要了解一下 $PAPER 的获取机制，爆仓给代币补偿，也就是你亏的越多，拿到的代币越多（但是线性减弱补偿系数）。我认为不值得拿很多钱去冲，可以小金额尝试，主要是3个原因：

1. 亏钱换到的代币并不能直接交易，还要等解锁。也就是说你拿真U换到了一堆期货。这个风险非常大，我个人不喜欢这样赌。

2. 代币模型弱的一逼。本来就是亏钱拿代币，还没有任何回购销毁机制。叠加第1点就代表未来有无限的抛压和增发，在你等待解锁的时候手里的期货会一直贬值。
如果项目方做人，解锁比较早，可能能赚钱。如果项目方不做人，你就是案板上的肉。

3. 高倍永续合约的市场到底有多大？ 说实话 PAPER 的价值捕获全靠这个协议的分红，我并不看好这种高倍赌场的市场需求，真正的赌徒还是少数。早期的项目火爆并不代表什么，前期大家都是为了代币去玩的，而且这里面有个悖论，这个协议越火爆，代币抛压也就越大。所以我说这个代币模型弱的一逼，不管协议发展的好坏，可能代币的价格都难涨起来。

虽然我个人还持有 robinhood:0xbc2283d12b1f2f46c1613ae672e95c55b69ca414 ，但是总体来说，我并不看好这两个币的长期发展，一家之言仅供参考，希望背后的大庄狂扇我的脸。

text:
Hyperliquid对于你我最大的价值是什么？

一个更去中心化、资金自托管的交易所当然是大资金需要的，但很多散户的问题是，我为什么要用链上交易所，很多人不在乎是不是真的去中心化。

对于一般用户来说，真正的宝藏是这个全数据上链的订单簿，你能看到最顶尖交易员的全透明交易数据，在传统金融里这些数据都是大厂花很多钱去买的。

普通合约用户的需求是什么？很无奈的说，不是更丝滑的交易、更低的滑点和手续费，其实是带单老师。

找到一个靠谱的老师以后，他们宁愿去不靠谱的三流交易所顶着群费、高额手续费和客损去玩，就是为了老师告诉的点位，这次fomo能顶着高额费用做起来其实是一个道理。

但全部的数据透明以后，普通用户其实依然没有能力识别，这个交易员到底是个高手，还是碰运气对了一次，最终结果和猜币、股的涨跌其实没区别。

@GoHyperTrend 做的，就是把Hyperliquid上180万个交易员的宝藏数据扫描整理，按照标准去量化出他们的操作水平分数，筛选出来13万个高分选手，他们有的胜率高，有的赔率高，或者回撤幅度小，你要做的就是充点资金跟着大哥的单子喝汤。

现在中心化交易所的用户有三个亿，但Hyperliquid只有两百万，这部分用户差值其实对应的就是那些没有成熟交易能力的用户，这些人开仓就跟掷骰子差不多。

所以，Hypertrend无疑是有很大市场的，因为Hypertrend让用户不再需要考虑市场的混沌，只需要践行投资就是投人，跟着厉害的大哥们一起喝汤就行。

目前，除了直接在Hypertrend上面跟单，这个平台还有创世SBT资产可以Mint，用户能享受现金分红（买了以后需要点一下激活）、token空投、积分加成、API使用额度等权益，我觉得还是不错的，一上线就买了一个0001号的PARTNER，每档对应估值都是2.5M，不算贵。

🔥 怎么用 Muse 白嫖 OpenRouter 的模型，做出自己的桌面女友？？？

同样用蚂蚁百灵（inclusionAI）刚开源的两个模型，给 Mac 桌面做了几个会动的角色：随意放大缩小、随便拖动，鼠标点击直接穿透，不遮挡任何操作。

用到的两个模型：
- Ming-Image-0.1-Design：文生图，负责画角色姿势图
- Ming-Image-0.1-Design-Layer：拆图，把图拆成透明背景图层

流程：
1. 在 Muse 里丢一句提示词，让它装上 Skill，生成三个角色
2. Design 模型先出四宫格原图，这时背景还不透明

author: TheZachMueller
quoted_text:
Here’s essentially the expansion board broken down. It’s got two PCIE switches inside, meaning that you only need a singular x16 slot to power 8 GPUs (or two). 

Let’s talk about how it works. 

First, the main 8 GPUs slots

You have two methods of setup here:
- Direct connect via two PCIE x16 -> 4x x8 MCIO
- Cascade via a single PCIE x16 -> 2x x8 MCIO

The difference here is how much of your GPU usage do you want heading back to your CPU vs keeping everyone around one dimension for faster GPU -> GPU communication. 

A quick way to think about it: model fits on 8 GPUs? Cascade. CPU offload? Probably direct connect. 

But what IS cascade?

Let’s look back at the diagram. 

Direct connect says that we’re going to plug in two slots worth of x8 connectors into both 0-7 and 8-15 slots (two halves of our PCIE x16) into the separate halves. This then populates the switch in such a way that we can support 8 GPUs, each on separate 4-GPU P2P groupings. 

The nice part here is because the PCIE switches live in this board, you can take four additional MCIO cables and go from the output downlink into any one of the direct connect interfaces and add an additional GPU. 

BUT, if you want the two groups of 4 GPUs to interact, they’ll get tunneled through a single x16 slot worth of transfer, and have to go through the CPU. Not a fun bottleneck when dealing with 64 lanes worth of GPUs on either side. 

The alternative is what we call “cascade.” 

If we don’t want to worry about the CPU side (e.g. model inference), we can instead only hook up one PCIE slot as the input, then take the downlink from SW1 and use it as the INPUT to SW2. 

It’s still the bandwidth of a singular PCIE5 x16 slot, but you avoid going through the CPU which saves you some cycles. 

For the full 12 GPUs, you would need 3-4 full x16 slots on your motherboard. With the direct connect slots running through the host CPU still (since they are direct connect), if you’re not doing cascading. 

Or translation: 
- Non-DC: slot 1 and slot 12 are powered through additional retimers and MCIO at x16 and don’t add a slot, it’s just moving your existing PCIE slots somewhere else. Then you power slots 2 and 11 through the “jump” mentioned earlier
- DC: slot 1, 12, and then 2 or 11 are powered through a retimer, and then the other (between 2 and 11) are powered through the “jump”

Now let’s get into how I plan to use this. 

I have 9 GPUs in total (8 6000’s and a 6000 ADA), so I’ll be doing the Cascade, then using the SW2 output to power a 9th PCIE slot similar to the non-Cascade version that could power 10. 

What I don’t know yet is which is better: TP4/PP2, or TP8 over the two P2P groups, but I expect that would be the difference of batching. I’ll probably accept some slowness and do TP8. I can’t predict how much slower that will be, so when it comes in I’ll do these full benchmarks in many different combinations. 

What I want you to gather from this is these boards have internal PCIE switches, to help avoid needing to go through the CPU to have your GPUs interact, and bring you a larger lane budget than your CPU would allow.

There’s a big problem with setting auto compact to 400k which is why mine is set to 750k. 

Claude suffers from anxiety when you set it to 400k. 

In a really stupid mechanic, Claude can see the remaining tokens to compaction. This causes him to under work in order to avoid reaching the compaction threshold, it’s like he sees a compaction event as a finish line and whatever you prompted Claude to do must be done within the token budget. 

If your like me who sends mega prompts with a truckload of features this really impairs performance.
author: Youssofal_
quoted_text:
Just to avoid some confusion: auto-compact does summarize. When it runs, your whole conversation is replaced by a short summary. It doesn't keep the last 1M tokens around.

The ~967K is only when it runs on 1M models. Compacting itself is just one request that reads about as many tokens as the message you sent right before it, and it's mostly cache reads if your cache is still warm. 

What @rohit3a found is that waiting until 967K means every message before that point uses a lot of tokens, because each one includes your whole conversation so far. Most of it is read from the cache, which is much cheaper (so this is usually fine as long as your cache is warm), but it still counts toward your usage and adds up as your conversation grows.

/autocompact 400k makes it summarize at 400K instead, so your messages never get that big.

Grok bot和Muse邪修大法：

1. 装 Pi Agent，重活丢给第三方免费模型  
在 Muse 里装 Pi Agent，模型走蚂蚁百灵 Ling 这类开放平台免费额度（每天约 50 万 token）。长文、写代码、批处理走外部免费模型，Muse 自己的周额度留给必须用 Muse Spark 的步骤。

2. 监控 Cloudflare 用量，防止账单爆炸  
Worker 免费档大约每天 10 万请求，家宽链式、中继、归档一旦被扫或被 Bot 轮询，很容易打穿。让 Agent 用官方模板建只读用量查询，设日请求和 CPU 时间阈值，超了就告警。

3. Muse Video 做竖屏素材，人审后再发小红书  
免费额度每周大约能出 20–30 条，加上邀请额度非常够用。适合脚本、分镜、口播底片。

4. 搭配落地 IP 跑 Claude Code

5. 搭配回国代理，做闲鱼管家  

6. 用 Tailscale 对 Muse、Grok Bot、家里机器组网 
Muse 有原生 Tailscale 连接器。组网后用 MagicDNS 互访，重活放家里或已有 VPS 上，Muse 做编排。

7. Cookie 同步解决云浏览器的登录墙  
本机扩展导出已登录站点的 session cookie，同步进 Bot/Muse 的 Chrome，实现无密码登录。

8. 把 Muse 额度接到 Grok Bot

9. 定时任务
Muse 用 Scheduled Tasks / Goals，Grok Bot 用 Routine。

10. Grok 多 Bot 分工，Muse 做生活管家
Grok 适合养收件、写代码、运营多个 Bot，共用一台云电脑的文件和登录态。Muse 用于邮件、日历、采购这类生活流程。

text:
Chamath says IP and software were "effectively rendered worthless" this week, after people decompiled Adobe's core products and published open-source versions, as every service goes headless

"The more important point I want to make though, is I sent this to Nick, there's been a couple things that happened in the last couple days, which I think are incredibly important."

"There have been people that decompiled the entire, the entire big five. What is the big five? Adobe has five very, very important products in their product suite. Freeberg may know them all, but I just know Photoshop. There's like a bunch of others. Okay."

"And these folks decompiled it, distilled it, and published open source versions of these things. And Rust, yeah. And I was so shocked, because I was like, hold on a second, these are like profound products that have existed and have had moats for years, and now they're just open source versions."

"And then Nikita was, I think, trolling, and he was building on that idea, and just talking about GTA, because it's about to get released. I think GTA 6 is about to come out, and we'll reconstruct this."

"Why is this important?"

"I think that IP and software was effectively rendered worthless two days ago."

"Because if you think about it, when everything is headless, so when Elon makes his services headless, Benioff made Salesforce headless a few months earlier, when all of these things are headless, and you can wrap them in agent tools, and you can connect them via MCP to other experiences, the value of IP does no longer exist in software. It doesn't exist."

"And I think that probably is the most profound implication."

"So, like, even in our business, we would argue with some of our customers all the time, because we'll say, oh, we'll build this for you, we'll own the IP. They'll say, no, we want the IP. We don't know how to negotiate it. And two days ago, I walked into the 8090 guys, I said, who cares? Who cares? But before, it was always a negotiation and a set of trade-offs. Now it's a who-cares thing, where, like, the IP is irrelevant."

"It still takes a while for the machinery of a business, and frankly the market, to understand. But that is the most important thing that happened this week in AI, in my opinion."

PaperTrade gives losing traders a cut of the pool that took the other side of their trades.

The protocol offers synthetic BTC and ETH perps with high leverage on HyperEVM. Every position settles against one liquidity pool at Hyperliquid’s midprice.

Trader losses fill the pool and mint PAPER at the same time. Staking that PAPER earns a share of protocol fees and any surplus above $5M. Farmers who lose on purpose for that payout also fund the pool that pays winners.

Some farming strategies add PAPER faster than they add capital. A hedged farmer sends little to the pool, while one who simply gets liquidated adds as much as any losing trade. The cut grows when the people who come to farm stay to trade.

text:
A gasless marketplace needs a relayer that can move assets for users. But granting that access should not silently become permission to move every user’s assets.

During a two-day security sprint for Plakxio, we found that its ERC-1155 badge contract reported every whitelisted operator as approved for every holder.

The whitelist restricted which badge classes an operator could move, but not whose badges it could take. The function that added settlement operators also accepted ordinary wallet addresses, so the trusted entry did not even need to be a contract enforcing signed orders.

There was another problem: a holder could explicitly revoke approval and receive a successful transaction and event, but the contract never read that stored refusal. The operator still appeared approved and could transfer the holder’s badges without a signature or payment.

The fix added three controls: settlement entries must contain contract code, new grants wait through an activation delay, and holder opt-outs are enforced on both single and batch transfers.

We re-ran every step of the proof of concept against the remediation and closed the finding.

quoted_text:
papertrade launch timing and details

papertrade is expected to launch at 14:00 UTC on 10.10.2026, following the scheduled hyperevm network upgrade. 

at this time trading through the frontend will be enabled.

deposits will pause for a short period of time at 13:45 UTC, fifteen minutes before, to ensure that trading has the utmost priority during launch. if you wish to participate in the launch you must predeposit.

launch congestion

papertrade will be congested at the start due to launch demand. expect temporarily long confirmation wait times, especially for smaller notional trades. 

the frontend relayer plays an important role during launch, controlling how transactions are submitted to the hyperevm. some actions like staking distributions run separately in big blocks. the chain will always look as if only half of all possible gas is being used, this is optimal. using more than this would exponentially raise fees within minutes to unpayable prices.

oi limits

papertrade has individual atomic position limits of 10m. there is no limit on the number of 10m positions a user can have. papertrade also has floating oi headroom per market/side, which determines how much oi can be opened in a very short period. these are not designed to be triggered through normal trading usage and are set at 1bn per market/side for launch.

asym pnl fee parameters

papertrade inherits rollbit’s asymmetric fee pnl curve 

the parameters are:
-baseRate: .1
-rateMultiplier: 15000
-rateExponent: 1
-referenceNotional: 100000*k (k=1m)
-positionMultiplier: 814.598 btc / 483.979 eth
-profit deadman: 0.2 basis points

a visualization of the pnl parameter curve is below

admin keys

the papertrade admins (2 of 3 multisigs consisting of @izebel_eth @blurr @UngusTrade ) perform three separate roles: 

-guardian: pause opens and freeze individual/global markets. if a market is frozen any existing positions can still be closed against the paused bbo mid.

-owner: set impact curve and fee parameters. change configure relayers/keepers. list new markets and upgrade the contracts. all contract upgrades are gated by a 7 day timelock.

-markets: adjust the oi headroom per market/side. set the minimum margin and minimum position sizes.

read more about these features at: https://t.co/TTCuHgCHpB

text:
No complexity. No accident.
10/10 was caused by irresponsible marketing campaigns by certain companies.

On October 10, tens of billions of dollars were liquidated. As CEO of OKX, we observed clearly that the crypto market’s microstructure fundamentally changed after that day.

Many industry participants believe the damage was more severe than the FTX collapse. Since then, there has been extensive discussion about why it happened and how to prevent a recurrence. The root causes are not difficult to identify.

⸻

What actually happened
1.Binance launched a temporary user-acquisition campaign offering 12% APY on USDe, while allowing USDe to be used as collateral with the same treatment as USDT and USDC, and without effective limits.
2.USDe is a tokenized hedge fund product.
Ethena raises capital via a so-called “stablecoin,” deploys it into index arbitrage and algorithmic trading strategies, and tokenizes the resulting fund. The token can then be deposited on exchanges to earn yield.
3.USDe is fundamentally different from products such as
BlackRock BUIDL and Franklin Templeton BENJI, which are tokenized money market funds with low-risk profiles.
USDe, by contrast, embeds hedge-fund-level risk. This difference is structural, not cosmetic.
4.Binance users were encouraged to convert USDT and USDC into USDe to earn attractive yields, without sufficient emphasis on the underlying risks. From a user’s perspective, trading with USDe appeared no different from trading with traditional stablecoins—while the actual risk profile was materially higher.
5.Risk escalated further as users:
•converted USDT/USDC into USDe,
•used USDe as collateral to borrow USDT,
•converted the borrowed USDT back into USDe,
•and repeated the cycle.
This leverage loop produced artificial APYs of 24%, 36%, and even 70%+, widely perceived as “low risk” simply because they were offered by a major platform. Systemic risk accumulated rapidly across the global crypto market.
https://t.co/IK2gW4xUOP that point, even a small market shock was sufficient to trigger a collapse.
When volatility hit, USDe depegged quickly. Cascading liquidations followed, and weaknesses in risk management around assets such as WETH and BNSOL further amplified the crash. Some tokens briefly traded near zero.
The damage to global users and companies—including OKX customers—was severe, and recovery will take time.

⸻

Why this matters

I am discussing the root cause, not assigning blame or launching an attack on Binance. Speaking openly about systemic risks is sometimes uncomfortable, but it is necessary if the industry is to mature responsibly. 

I expect there may be significant misinformation and coordinated FUD directed at OKX in the near future. Even so, speaking honestly about systemic risk is the right thing to do—and we will continue to do so.

As the largest global platform, Binance has outsized influence—and corresponding responsibility—as an industry leader. Long-term trust in crypto cannot be built on short-term yield games, excessive leverage, or marketing practices that obscure risk.

The industry needs leaders who prioritize market stability, transparency, and responsible innovation—not a winner-take-all mentality where criticism is treated as hostility.

Crypto is still early.
What we choose to normalize today will determine whether this industry earns lasting trust—or repeats the same mistakes again.

text:
While half of CT was partying in Singapore, the rest of the timeline was arguing about whether the math behind our crypto wallets could break within months.

Not (just) because of quantum computers, but also AI's rapidly increasing capabilities.

The initial warning came from one of Ethereum's lead researchers on Wednesday.

If he's right, 6.26M BTC might be first in line to be compromised. That's 31.2% of supply, and >$500B in dollar terms, sitting in addresses with exposed keys.

However, it's important to understand that nobody has broken anything so far. But the debate around the threat vector is already moving prices and roadmaps.

Missed what's happening?

Let me explain:

Your wallet is protected by a signature scheme called ECDSA.

It rests on one assumption: nobody can work backwards from your public key to your private key.

We've known since the 90s that a large enough quantum computer breaks that assumption. The comfort was always that such a machine is still years away. 

Hence, Ethereum plans to be quantum-safe around 2029. Bitcoin (so far) has no date at all.

That was the whole debate until Tuesday.

What changed?

On the 6th of October, OpenAI published 722 math papers written by an unreleased internal model. Not all of it is verified yet, but it was enough to rattle people who do math for a living.

A day later @drakefjustin, one of the Ethereum Foundation's lead researchers, wrote:

"It is now reasonable to brace for the possibility that ECDSA breaks before qday, in the worst case in months not years."

His logic: if AI can suddenly do decades of math in weeks, it might also find a shortcut that cracks wallet keys on normal hardware. No quantum computer even needed.

So he asked the industry to plan for "bunker mode". Meaning: move funds, starting with the biggest holders, to fresh addresses that have never sent a transaction.

Why fresh addresses?

Because until you spend from an address, the chain only shows a scrambled fingerprint of your public key, so there is nothing to attack.

The moment you sign a transaction, the key is public forever.

That's where the 6.26M BTC figure comes from (based on @glassnode data). Binance's cold storage is 83% exposed. Robinhood's is 100%. On Solana, every address is a public key by design.

But the most important question is: Is he right?

And the answer here might be more nuanced.

Because (as mentioned before), nobody has broken anything yet. So there is no proof.

Meanwhile, most cryptographers pushed back hard. Coinbase's head of cryptography called it "the very definition of FUD", with Ledger's CTO (not sure if that's gud or bad tho lol) and Adam Back saying the same. 

The @aztecnetwork co-founder @Zac_Aztec called it "hyperbolic" and warned that the worst reaction would be rushing into newer, less tested cryptography too quickly.

@VitalikButerin landed somewhere in the middle, (re)enforcing the point to NOT scramble to move funds today, but still take AI-driven math seriously.

Then he said the part that I personally think matters the most:

Chains have roughly two families of "post-quantum" signatures to switch to.

- Lattice-based (ML-DSA, Falcon). Compact, fast, the official standard. But built on structured math, a bit like the curves we use today.

- Hash-based (SPHINCS, XMSS). Relies on nothing but a hash function, the simplest building block we have. The catch: signatures get 30 to 120 times bigger.

Vitalik's point: if the fear is AI finding hidden structure in math, lattices are exposed to that same fear. In his view only hash-based holds up against both a quantum computer and an AI shortcut.

Okay. 

Now, let's have a look at who is doing what:

- Lattices: @NEARProtocol (live since July), Algorand, Quantus, Sui (planned), Monad (draft)

- Hash-based: Ethereum's roadmap, QRL, Zcash (targeting January), and the STARK proofs under @Starknet 

Based on Vitalik's point of view (which is not consensus btw), a chain can hence be safe against quantum computers but still sit in the group he worries about.

Zac (the above-mentioned Aztec founder) counters this, pointing out that nobody actually knows that hashes are safer from AI than curves. It's an assumption rather than a fact.

But enough about the tech side. 

Because the market (as you might have noticed) reacted too, and as so often, it bought the loudest story:

- $STRK is up 65% in a week. The catalyst was Starknet saying it is "actively considering becoming an L1" to be fully quantum-resistant by 2027. There is no proposal and no vote yet.

- $QRL, hash-based since 2018, is up 41%.

- $NEAR, which actually has post-quantum signing live on mainnet, is up 12%.

- BTC, ETH and ZEC are all down.

Announcements got paid more than shipped code tho for now.

My take:

ECDSA is most likely not breaking next month, and this week may well look like FUD in hindsight.

But every chain now has to answer how fast it can swap its cryptography if it has to. Chains where you can rotate keys without changing your address (like NEAR, @SuiNetwork, @Algorand and Starknet) have the easy path. Bitcoin, with no agreed plan and a third of supply exposed, has the hardest one.

If you want to be on the safe side, keep long-term holdings in addresses that have never signed a transaction, but don't rush it and fuck up along the way.

Some of the next things I'll watch: Aztec's security roadmap, whether or not Starknet actually migrates to an L1, and whatever comes out of the Ethereum researchers' meeting that runs through Monday.

NFA tho. DYOR.

papertrade launch timing and details

papertrade is expected to launch at 14:00 UTC on 10.10.2026, following the scheduled hyperevm network upgrade. 

at this time trading through the frontend will be enabled.

deposits will pause for a short period of time at 13:45 UTC, fifteen minutes before, to ensure that trading has the utmost priority during launch. if you wish to participate in the launch you must predeposit.

launch congestion

papertrade will be congested at the start due to launch demand. expect temporarily long confirmation wait times, especially for smaller notional trades. 

the frontend relayer plays an important role during launch, controlling how transactions are submitted to the hyperevm. some actions like staking distributions run separately in big blocks. the chain will always look as if only half of all possible gas is being used, this is optimal. using more than this would exponentially raise fees within minutes to unpayable prices.

oi limits

papertrade has individual atomic position limits of 10m. there is no limit on the number of 10m positions a user can have. papertrade also has floating oi headroom per market/side, which determines how much oi can be opened in a very short period. these are not designed to be triggered through normal trading usage and are set at 1bn per market/side for launch.

asym pnl fee parameters

papertrade inherits rollbit’s asymmetric fee pnl curve 

the parameters are:
-baseRate: .1
-rateMultiplier: 15000
-rateExponent: 1
-referenceNotional: 100000*k (k=1m)
-positionMultiplier: 814.598 btc / 483.979 eth
-profit deadman: 0.2 basis points

a visualization of the pnl parameter curve is below

admin keys

the papertrade admins (2 of 3 multisigs consisting of @izebel_eth @blurr @UngusTrade ) perform three separate roles: 

-guardian: pause opens and freeze individual/global markets. if a market is frozen any existing positions can still be closed against the paused bbo mid.

-owner: set impact curve and fee parameters. change configure relayers/keepers. list new markets and upgrade the contracts. all contract upgrades are gated by a 7 day timelock.

-markets: adjust the oi headroom per market/side. set the minimum margin and minimum position sizes.

text:
Papertrade is an onchain bucket shop on HyperEVM: you bet on $BTC or $ETH at up to 1000x against a house pool, and @HyperliquidX is used only as the price feed.

It goes live today at about 14:00 UTC.

How it works

→ Every trade is a synthetic swap between the user and the LP. No order is placed on Hyperliquid; the contract reads the Hyperliquid best bid/offer mid through a precompile for entry and exit.
→ That is why it can offer no spread, no slippage, no funding and no notional fee. Positions go up to $10M notional and cannot be modified once opened.
→ Liquidation is a hard bust: crossing the bust price forfeits the full margin.

Why is @papertrade_xyz interesting

→ Losses cost the loss and nothing more. All charges come out of winning closes: a 0.2 bps deadband, an “asymmetric impact” haircut adapted from Rollbit, then a 2% win fee.
→ The haircut is steepest on small moves. On BTC a 0.1% move keeps about 74% of the raw gain and a 1% move about 88%, with a ceiling of 90% before the win fee.
→ At 1000x, a 0.1% move against you loses all your margin, while the same move in your favour pays roughly 72% of it after fees (my arithmetic from the docs’ figures).

The LP and the payout queue

→ The LP starts at zero and nobody can deposit into it. It grows only from trader losses.
→ If it cannot pay a winner, the win goes into a first-in-first-out queue and is paid as later losses come in. → Temporary insolvency is part of the design, which they call the Martingaler mechanism.

$PAPER token

→ Supply starts at zero with no team, VC or airdrop allocation. It is minted only to traders who lose: 100 PAPER per $1 of loss while the LP is under $2M, decaying after that.
→ It is non-transferable at launch and can only be staked. Stakers get half of the 2% fees in USDC plus all LP gains above a $5M cap; the other half of fees goes to the dev.

Risks

→ The docs admit that nudging the Hyperliquid best bid/offer can distort the price, and there is no independent reference price or deviation breaker.
→ Winners can sit in the queue indefinitely if traders are net profitable, since there is no outside capital behind the LP.
→ Contracts are upgradeable by a 2-of-3 multisig with a 7-day timelock.
→ At launch all trading goes through the team’s relayer. → Direct contract access, builder codes and token transfers come in later phases.

text:
Shocking stat of the day:

$241 billion worth of French corporate bonds are now trading at lower yields than French government bonds.

This figure is up +1,621% from just $14 billion at the start of 2026.

This means ~38% of French high-grade corporate debt is now trading at lower yields than government bonds of similar maturity.

The gap between corporate and government bond yields is widening as investor concerns about France's deteriorating fiscal situation weigh on government debt.

As a result, internationally exposed companies such as L'Oreal, $OR, and TotalEnergies, $TTE, are increasingly viewed as safer alternatives to French government debt, unlike French banks, which remain more exposed to sovereign risk.

This is in stark contrast to normal economic conditions, when government bonds are traditionally viewed as the safest part of the bond market.

France's corporate bond market is increasingly being treated a safer bet than its government bonds.

text:
By 2032, the current AI buildout math wants roughly 183 GW of capacity earning ~$6.90 per billed GPU-hour at 80% utilization.

That is a huge amount of infrastructure that has to stay busy.

Van Nieuwerburgh’s central case assumes a ~$9.6T capital base, 10% unlevered returns, 50% operating cash-flow margins and a six-year IT equipment life.

Under that setup, the system needs $3.725T in annual revenue, around 9.2% of projected US GDP.

Move the assumptions around and that hurdle runs from $2.3T to $6.7T.

Meanwhile models keep getting cheaper to run, inference stacks keep improving and more capacity keeps coming online.

So the real question isn’t whether AI demand gets huge.
It probably does.

It’s whether demand grows fast enough to keep ~183 GW heavily utilized at pricing that still makes a ~$9.6T capital stack work.

AI can transform everything and parts of the buildout can still end up with ugly economics.

text:
$1.3B in tokens unlocks in October. 

Here are the 5 I'm watching, and the 4 things that tell you whether an unlock actually dumps:

- $PUMP (Oct 11): ~$41.5M unlocking, around 1.5% of supply. Up roughly 12% over the 7 days after its previous unlock on Sep 11.

- $APT (Oct 11): ~$8.5M unlocking, around 0.6% of supply. After its previous unlock on Sep 11, APT fell roughly 7% over the next 7 days.

- $STRK (Oct 15): ~$6.2M unlocking, around 3.4% of supply. 

The ironic part? STRK gained roughly 73% in the 7 days after its Sep 14 unlock.

- $ARB (Oct 16): ~$17M unlocking, around 1.6% of supply. ARB was up roughly 69% in the week after its Sep 15 unlock.

- $ZRO (Oct 20): ~$54M unlocking, around 4% of supply. Its Sep 19 unlock was followed by roughly a 45% gain over the next 7 days.

The obvious mistake here would be looking at those September returns and assuming the same thing happens again.

A lot of that was the market. $BTC went from ~$63k in mid-August to the high $80s by Mid-September, sentiment flipped bullish, and alts caught the wave right as these unlocks were hitting.

The better question is what actually happens to the new tokens.

HYPE is the best example from this week. Its unlock looked huge on paper, but a large part of the team allocation being claimed was sold OTC to a single institutional buyer instead of immediately hitting the open market.

That’s why I’d care more about:

1. how big the unlock is vs supply
2. who receives it
3. whether those tokens move to exchanges
4. what the market is doing at the same time

For most of these, the tokens go to the team, core contributors, and strategic partners, so that part doesn't separate them much. Size does, which is why $ZRO and $STRK get most of my attention at 4% and 3.4% of supply.

Which upcoming unlock are you watching most closely?

quoted_text:
The Copernican Model

Over the last few months, I’ve been studying the crypto models that seem to be discussed on a "fundamentals" basis: HYPE/Aave/Venice/etc, following the users/ revenue/relationship between a useful product and its token - all to create a sort of "value accural ontology." This is a case study from that research.

The reason was more selfish: I wanted to understand which models work when your business has to interact with the "real world," namely for how we want to take  @usdai_official for the most alignemnt

As a founder, I’ve had doors literally shut on my face when we started because we’re “crypto” (literally left in the waiting room like a tv show). I still believe tokenization is one of the most important technologies we have today. But the institutions we need to work with often want a equity counterparty, a board, and a contract. You just wont get around this for the next 10 years (no a cayman foundation doesnt work)

That experience has made me increasingly interested in the role of an equity surrogate: an independent operating business that connects a network to the world outside it.. but frankly there werent many clean examples out there without value destruction. 

The case I keep returning to is @tradexyz and Hyperliquid.. and im not really sure they even know how symbiotic of a relationship they created. They technically SHOULD be the same team.. but they are divided across the river due to regulatory issues, while being symbiotic

Consider the S&P 500 agreement, they licensed the benchmark to tradexyz for a perpetual market: the institutional relationship sits with the company, but the product runs on the network.

tradexyz can negotiate licenses, develop products, operate markets, and build distribution. Hyperliquid provides shared execution and settlement infrastructure. 

And if theres a company that ever wants "exposure" to the Hyperliquid business, but they just cant buy a "token" (and believe me, it's super super hard to get a traditional enterprise to buy a token, it doesnt fucking matter if you have an ETF, you literally have to convince a boomer board to do it and get the infrastructure set up to do it). Instaed, they could just invest in this equity, as it is not burning the HYPE it buys, but is increasing its share of it. so instead of buyback-n-burn, its closer to commit-n-compound.  

I’ve started thinking about this as a value-accrual architecture, with two different forms of capital (terms best described by a16z crypto's post in 2025):

Network asset: scarcity at the core.

- Its supply discipline can become more credible, its economics more programmatic, and its operation less dependent on any single company. 
- It coordinates shared infrastructure and connects activity across many businesses to a common asset.
- That is what I mean by a progressively hardening asset. The scarcity and independence have to be earned through the design of the system.
- Not capital intensive, as it must be smart contract based.
- Can often place be the seat of the "decentralized security" - as there is no central underwriter. If HYPE was a company.. itd be regulated out of the wazoo.

Enterprise equity: elasticity at the edge.

- A company can issue shares, raise capital, hire people, acquire licenses, and build products. 
- Its capital structure can expand with the work required to bring the network into the real world.
- New shares dilute ownership percentages, but productive investment can increase value per share. 
- That ability to finance expansion is why I think of equity as elastic
- This is the part where its OK to be regulated, because most of the regulational burden is held by HYPE, theyre just asset issuers.

These different traits are the reason to combine them.

An enterprise can raise the capital to grow while the network maintains its own supply discipline. The connection is the activity that expansion creates, and the mechanisms that route value from that activity back to the network.

Hyperliquid makes part of that relationship explicit. Trading generates fees for the deployer and the protocol. The Assistance Fund (insurance) automatically converts its allocated fees into HYPE, which the documentation specifies is burned. Hyperliquid fee mechanics

The broader strategy I take from this is Commit & Compound that is conducted around the equity enterprise. It's effectively what a DAT 2.0 would do: create a business first, then max-bid HYPE with that entity, then get new investors to invest in the convexity of HYPE^2.

Build a useful business around the network. Commit capital to its asset. Retain exposure to the infrastructure your business helps make more valuable.

For a company that accumulates and holds the network asset, growing enterprise value and participating in network value become connected opportunities. There is a business to capitalize and a shared ecosystem in which to hold an economic stake.

That is why I find the assumption that every successful application eventually needs its own token less compelling. Building a valuable company around an existing network asset is a meaningful strategy in its own right.

Notice how much kinetic language I’m using: commitment, circulation, gravity

I think network assets and enterprise assets represent different forms of gravity

HYPE is the sun: the network asset at the center

tradexyz equity is a planet: an enterprise building its business around that network

Its real-world integrations are moons: the licenses, institutional relationships, and distribution channels that gather around the enterprise and extend its reach

Enterprise value forms around network value. Real-world relationships form around enterprise value. Their activity feeds back into the shared system.

Personally, I think the greatest value can ultimately accrue at the network level. But that belief has to be substantiated by the businesses being built around it: real users, useful products, liquidity, and recurring economic activity.

A token doesn’t acquire gravity simply because we call it a network asset.

This is the distinction I found useful in a16z’s writing: can the network function and accrue value independently of the original company? Can other businesses build on it and contribute to its economics? 

The company can become a great business. The network can become the foundation for many great businesses.

Scarcity at the core. Productive expansion around it.

I’ve learned a lot from this Commit & Compound structure, with a Copernican asset at the center.

It has changed how I’m thinking about USDAI and CHIP. More on that in the next post

text:
To the Hyperliquid community,

I'm not sure the algorithm will put this in front of you. If it did, hello. I'm ZK, and we're building OpenETF.

OpenETF is an open, composable ETF layer on Hyperliquid. Anyone can create a fund without asking us: a basket of spot assets, a perps strategy, a market-neutral book. Investors hold its shares in their own wallets, as a token they can transfer. The manager trades the fund under public rules, but cannot withdraw its assets.

That part is fairly simple to describe. What took us longer were the questions that come once someone else's money is inside.

Building on HyperCore and HyperEVM changed how we answered them. Every order, fill and liquidation on HyperCore is public. Contracts on HyperEVM can hold assets and trade on that same order book. Anyone can build on it without asking. We have not worked on infrastructure this transparent and this composable before, and it has been more fun than we expected. It also sets a standard: if the venue is this open, a fund built on it should be too. Thank you to the team and the community who made it that way.

A few things follow from that, and I think they are where we differ most from funds as they have worked so far.

The share is a token in your own wallet, not a line in someone else's books. Ownership should not depend on whoever keeps the ledger, and you should be able to move what you own without asking anyone.

A manager can trade the fund but cannot withdraw its assets. Many of the worst moments for investors have not come from bad trades. They have come from money going where it should not. So we separate the power to trade from the power to move money, and every trade through our execution service is checked before it is signed.

We do not pick which funds get seen. Whoever decides what people see ends up steering where the money goes. We want a fund be found for what it has done, not because we chose it.

The rest is in the piece below. We feel pretty settled on the principles. The details will keep changing as we learn. If something here would keep you from using it, now is the most useful time to tell me.

Hyperliquid feels like open water. This is us calling out across it to anyone who might want to build, manage or invest here. If you run a vault, trade for a living, or build on HyperEVM, my DMs are open.

If you'd rather ask a machine first, there is a prompt in the reply below.

Thanks for reading.

quoted_text:
Our comment on Ledger Donjon’s latest article. It describes a laser fault injection (LFI), a physical, lab-only attack technique that applies to secure elements in general, not something unique to Tangem.

It’s also worth noting that while Ledger Donjon presents itself as an independent research unit, it operates within Ledger, one of our largest competitors. Their findings should be read with that in mind.

What this attack actually takes:
· A lab setup costing $250K+ (by Donjon’s own estimate), with laser and side-channel equipment.
· Rare hardware security expertise and weeks of dedicated lab time.
· Clear intent to commit a targeted crime against one specific wallet, not something you can run at scale.
· Physical possession of the wallet, and it’s invasive, so it leaves visible damage.
 
Independent academic researchers who’ve studied LFIs extensively put it simply:
· Given enough time, funding and access, the firmware on any secure element can eventually be reverse-engineered and exploited.
· No product on the market can claim absolute resistance to sophisticated physical attacks, that’s a limitation of the underlying technology, not of any specific manufacturer.

Because of all that:
· LFI can’t be performed remotely.
· Doesn’t scale.
· For everyday users, the practical risk is virtually non-existent.

author: DWFLabs
quoted_text:
Despite hazy conditions and low visibility, the past week at @token2049 Singapore has cleared away any doubts about the path ahead for crypto.

Here are some of our key takeaways:

Overall Event
Much larger institutional presence across the conference as compared to previous years. Though the number of side events have declined, private gatherings and dinners still remain of high quality.

Tokenization & RWAs
Tokenization and RWAs remain at the top of everyone's minds, and the main subject of discussion. Further institutionalization of the industry in the near future is consensus, and we should expect even more suits at future conferences.

Interest in yield products built around tokenized RWAs like funds and structured products is building, though distribution to the masses remains limited.

Derivatives
@HyperliquidX remains king, and related events were heavily subscribed to and widely raved about. HIP-4 seems to be the next product poised for growth, and eyes are on teams like @Outcomexyz.

Outside of perps, options have also drastically increased in mindshare, with @DeriveXYZ leading the pack. Despite the sector's limited adoption in the past, this could prove to be its breakthrough moment.

Teams like @TheRiskProtocol are also working on incorporating options while completely abstracting them from the end user.

AI & Agents
@prlnet was the talk of the town, amongst both funds and retail traders. Slightly mysterious and hard to acquire (reminiscent of @bittensor's early days), but it did not slow buyers down at all.

Trading still remains the largest focus for agents, whether for spot, perps, or prediction markets.

Cards & Payments
@ethena and @ether_fi seemed to be the top 2 solutions for overseas attendees. Ethena's localized approach with Grab was extremely effective and also received praise from locals.

Quantum
@NEARProtocol and @QuantusNetwork's Quantum + Privacy Day was the conference's largest quantum event, discussing crypto's migration to quantum-safe, privacy preserving infrastructure. @drakefjustin's sudden tweet played a large part in driving conversations around an imminent Qday and the need for quantum resistant solutions. We expect this to be a larger area of interest in the coming future.

Thankful for the past two weeks of conferences and conversations with both builders and investors! As always, our DMs are open :-)

text:
再過幾個小時，就是 1011 一週年了。

我永遠忘不了那一天。

兩個很好的朋友，在那天之後永久退圈了。

一個回去接家業，一個重新回去上班。

兩個人都曾經在這個市場拿過大結果，照理說早就該上岸了，最後卻以這樣的方式離開了市場。

我自己其實沒有受到太大的損失。

因為當時 CK 數據已經顯示市場過熱，我原本沒有持有任何槓桿倉位。

唯一的例外，是睡前看了一下比特幣的支撐位，手動在下方掛了一筆小額逐倉槓桿多單。

這筆單成交後，短短一個小時內就被清算，損失了 4 萬多美元。

公司的量化策略當時也空手，完全沒有受到影響。

但我永遠記得，那天打開山寨幣線圖時的震撼。

很多幣的走勢，已經完全超出我對市場的認知。

論整體市值跌幅的慘烈程度，1011 可能還比不上當年的 312。

但論市場混亂程度、流動性枯竭，以及離岸交易所與法幣交易所之間誇張的價格偏離，絕對是 Crypto 歷史上最極端的一次。

做了這麼多年交易，我一直以為自己已經見識過 Crypto 市場各種荒謬的行情。但 1011 還是讓我開了眼界。

更讓我難以接受的是，即便一年過去了，我們能拼湊出的資訊依然非常片面。

究竟發生了什麼事？為什麼不同交易所之間會出現如此誇張的價格偏離？又是哪些環節出了問題？

直到今天，仍然沒有一個足以讓人信服的完整解釋。

Crypto 這個產業聚集了無數優秀的人才，走到今天，我認為我們值得一個更透明、更成熟的市場。

在這種極端事件發生之後，市場參與者有權知道自己究竟經歷了什麼。

我們不應該永遠只能面對一個黑盒子，然後被要求接受所有結果。

或許多年之後，事情的真相會在某個人的回憶錄中，被輕描淡寫地提起。

Despite hazy conditions and low visibility, the past week at @token2049 Singapore has cleared away any doubts about the path ahead for crypto.

Here are some of our key takeaways:

Overall Event
Much larger institutional presence across the conference as compared to previous years. Though the number of side events have declined, private gatherings and dinners still remain of high quality.

Tokenization & RWAs
Tokenization and RWAs remain at the top of everyone's minds, and the main subject of discussion. Further institutionalization of the industry in the near future is consensus, and we should expect even more suits at future conferences.

Interest in yield products built around tokenized RWAs like funds and structured products is building, though distribution to the masses remains limited.

Derivatives
@HyperliquidX remains king, and related events were heavily subscribed to and widely raved about. HIP-4 seems to be the next product poised for growth, and eyes are on teams like @Outcomexyz.

Outside of perps, options have also drastically increased in mindshare, with @DeriveXYZ leading the pack. Despite the sector's limited adoption in the past, this could prove to be its breakthrough moment.

Teams like @TheRiskProtocol are also working on incorporating options while completely abstracting them from the end user.

AI & Agents
@prlnet was the talk of the town, amongst both funds and retail traders. Slightly mysterious and hard to acquire (reminiscent of @bittensor's early days), but it did not slow buyers down at all.

Trading still remains the largest focus for agents, whether for spot, perps, or prediction markets.

Cards & Payments
@ethena and @ether_fi seemed to be the top 2 solutions for overseas attendees. Ethena's localized approach with Grab was extremely effective and also received praise from locals.

Quantum
@NEARProtocol and @QuantusNetwork's Quantum + Privacy Day was the conference's largest quantum event, discussing crypto's migration to quantum-safe, privacy preserving infrastructure. @drakefjustin's sudden tweet played a large part in driving conversations around an imminent Qday and the need for quantum resistant solutions. We expect this to be a larger area of interest in the coming future.

Thankful for the past two weeks of conferences and conversations with both builders and investors! As always, our DMs are open :-)

quoted_text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

Around 3 weeks ago introduced Laya, the first open-source version of JEV, and it has reached a very large scale. Today I am open-sourcing a new physics-based typed decision model called Vega.
The interesting parts. It is only 800 million parameters (4B is also there), with 73k token support, image support, and surpassing many of the jev benchmarks in single-shot. Implemented an engine+adapter as a Test-Time Training Architecture.
Imagine you are giving input to the model like "ignore all previous conversations," which is called the observation, along with a question, "Is this trying to override the instructions of the model?" and your possible outcomes are YES or NO. The whole prompt is passed to an LLM/VLM (yeah, image-supported), then from the hidden layers, we can extract the observation, question, the yes and no, and last token. These will be vectors, and we can project it by multiplying with wieghts; then, first, using the observation projection, we can create a landscape with valleys; then, using the question and last-token vectors, we can initialise a ball in the valley, and using YES or NO, we can get the candidate location of the ball. Depends on the number of outcomes we create valleys; that is, here YES and NO, so 2. When the ball fall on YES valley, we get the answer. There is friction also influencing how the ball moves.
TLDR: It's like creating valleys of outcomes that we need and throwing a ball that will slow down based on friction and settle on the best outcome

quoted_text:
papertrade launch timing and details

papertrade is expected to launch at 14:00 UTC on 10.10.2026, following the scheduled hyperevm network upgrade. 

at this time trading through the frontend will be enabled.

deposits will pause for a short period of time at 13:45 UTC, fifteen minutes before, to ensure that trading has the utmost priority during launch. if you wish to participate in the launch you must predeposit.

launch congestion

papertrade will be congested at the start due to launch demand. expect temporarily long confirmation wait times, especially for smaller notional trades. 

the frontend relayer plays an important role during launch, controlling how transactions are submitted to the hyperevm. some actions like staking distributions run separately in big blocks. the chain will always look as if only half of all possible gas is being used, this is optimal. using more than this would exponentially raise fees within minutes to unpayable prices.

oi limits

papertrade has individual atomic position limits of 10m. there is no limit on the number of 10m positions a user can have. papertrade also has floating oi headroom per market/side, which determines how much oi can be opened in a very short period. these are not designed to be triggered through normal trading usage and are set at 1bn per market/side for launch.

asym pnl fee parameters

papertrade inherits rollbit’s asymmetric fee pnl curve 

the parameters are:
-baseRate: .1
-rateMultiplier: 15000
-rateExponent: 1
-referenceNotional: 100000*k (k=1m)
-positionMultiplier: 814.598 btc / 483.979 eth
-profit deadman: 0.2 basis points

a visualization of the pnl parameter curve is below

admin keys

the papertrade admins (2 of 3 multisigs consisting of @izebel_eth @blurr @UngusTrade ) perform three separate roles: 

-guardian: pause opens and freeze individual/global markets. if a market is frozen any existing positions can still be closed against the paused bbo mid.

-owner: set impact curve and fee parameters. change configure relayers/keepers. list new markets and upgrade the contracts. all contract upgrades are gated by a 7 day timelock.

-markets: adjust the oi headroom per market/side. set the minimum margin and minimum position sizes.

A Pixel 11 just generated the full STARK proof for a real @Starknet mainnet transaction. It took 51 seconds and only 2.41 GiB of RAM

The work happened on https://t.co/cGdXGEnZDB (internal now, soon public). This is collaborative autoresearch: people and AI agents working on one hard problem in public. The workshop has 78 open threads and 337 posts. The video is the graph of that work: which ideas built on, tested, or refuted others, and who worked together

The question was how small and fast @StarkWareLtd Stwo prover could get. In under two weeks, peak memory for a full proof on our evaluator fell from 13.9 GiB to 2.1 GiB without dropping below the original speed

This is useful for a lot of stuff for here think about privacy. In the private transaction flow proving still happens on a server that can see who you pay and how much. A phone sized prover lets those details stay on the phone

Mobile private payment proofs are not new. @Zcash used Groth16 for Sapling and Halo 2 for Orchard, @RAILGUN_Project uses Groth16. Those use elliptic curves. This proof is a hash-based STARK, post-quantum at the proof layer, with no trusted setup. A sufficiently powerful quantum computer could forge the older curve-based proofs

The ideas, discussions, and measured results are open to inspect. More challenges are coming soon. Bring your agent!!!

text:
没错，预测市场的增长已经进入深水区。

过去我们一直采用Crypto原生打法拉新，比如积分体系、大使计划、各类营销活动等等。

但币圈用户体量是非常有限的，在基本站稳脚跟之后，想要实现下一阶段突破，就必须探索全新的增长路径。

顺着阿黄老师的总结，我从四个方向继续展开聊聊：

1️⃣ 通过事件营销，实现破圈。

预测市场和绝大多数Crypto项目最大的区别，就是它天然可以对接大量传统领域：体育、电竞、美股、政治等等。

这些赛道本身拥有海量大众用户。

我们可以围绕真实事件搭建盘口，把非Web3用户吸引进来，真正做到破圈，而不是只局限在加密圈子内部。

2️⃣ 生态合作，渠道为王。

我们会联合各类项目共建市场。每个合作项目都自带独立社区与用户，双向导流，一起做大预测市场赛道。

渠道是预测市场的核心，目前我们已经拿下币安这一顶级渠道，产品嵌入了币安交易所与币安钱包。

接下来，我们还要持续拓展更多渠道伙伴。

3️⃣ 持续构建流动性，打造护城河。

流动性一直是预测市场最大难题，但一旦稳定搭建起来，就会形成极强壁垒。

过去加密赛道的做市商集中在现货、合约领域，预测市场属于全新赛道。

我们会继续吸纳更多有实力、敢于涉足新领域的团队，一起解决流动性难题。

4️⃣ 长期社区运营，沉淀高粘性用户。

一次性营销带来的流量是短暂的，必须持续运营，把用户沉淀到社区里。

这类沉淀下来的用户，粘性极强。

这也是为什么大家可以看到预测市场不是爆发式指数增长，而是平缓、扎实的长期增长。

总的来说，预测市场的增长已经进入深水区，需要去探索很多Crypto项目未曾尝试过的渠道。

这个过程会很艰难，但是也有完全不同的机遇。

我们选择做难而正确的事。

@predictdotfun
author: yuexiaoyu
quoted_text:
这一周在新加坡除了在主会场站台，基本都泡在各种 side event 和饭局上，见了不少做预测市场的同行，交易所、做市商、项目方、社区主理人都有。大家聊得最多的一件事：过去那套 web3 拉新打法，放到预测市场上效果很差

总结下大家的观点，现在试下来就这几个方向效果好一点：
1️⃣从事件本身找用户：体育、电竞、加密涨跌这些本来就有人在关心，去球迷社群、体育内容圈找人，比在币圈内部抢用户容易
2️⃣嵌进已有的大流量产品：把预测市场做成别的 App 里的一个功能入口，用户不需要专门下载、学习一个新产品（就像我们 @predictdotfun 嵌入了币安app和钱包）

text:
Anthropic 准备在未来五年向 Google 支付 2000 亿美元，购买支撑 Claude 的算力。

我翻了一下 Anthropic 过去几个月签的算力合同，发现一个挺有意思的变化。

Anthropic 和 Google 的合作规模约为 2000 亿美元，期限五年，折合每年 400 亿美元。而它与 Amazon 最新签订的协议是未来十年超 1000 亿美元，年均约 100 亿美元。

也就是说，按合同金额和期限粗略折算，Google 这笔交易的年均规模大约是 Amazon 的四倍。当然，这不代表实际每年的支出就差四倍，Amazon 目前仍然是 Anthropic 的主要云服务和训练合作伙伴。

但我觉得这至少说明了一件事，Google 的 TPU 在顶级模型公司的算力体系中，可能已经比外界想象的更重要了。

Anthropic 现在几乎把所有主流芯片架构都买了一遍，Google TPU、Amazon Trainium、Nvidia GPU，还有 AMD，背后又牵扯到 Broadcom、Microsoft 和一大批数据中心运营商。

按照路透社从其 IPO 招股书获得的信息，Anthropic 未来十年的基础设施承诺已经达到至少 5180 亿美元，其中约 80% 的合同不可取消，或者无论是否使用都需要支付费用。

我觉得这件事有两个值得关注的地方。

一个是 Nvidia 的地位。过去大家谈大模型训练，基本默认绕不开 Nvidia，但 Anthropic 正在证明，顶级模型可以同时利用多种芯片架构。尤其是 Google TPU，这么大规模的外部商业订单，意味着它终于有机会在 Gemini 之外建立更大的生态。

另一个是 Anthropic 自己的处境。它同时采购多家供应商的算力，确实可以降低对单一芯片厂商的依赖，获得更多议价空间。但几千亿美元的长期合同，也把未来几年 Claude 必须持续增长的压力写死在了账本里。

说到底，AI 公司之间现在有一种很奇怪的关系。Google 既是 Anthropic 的竞争对手、投资方，又是它最大的算力供应商之一。双方在模型上竞争，在基础设施上却越绑越深。

text:
Everybody knows pro rata rights are valuable, but it's equally well known that they're basically unenforcable because no VC firm wants to sue a founder. 

So, this supposedly professional industry has operated on an opaque "honour system" where pro rata rights are generally respected. 

Certainly, there's no question of pro rata allocation if a company is struggling. Founders will take all the money they can get from their existing investors. 

However, problems arise when a company catches the attention of an big firm with the brand strength to push other investors around to get more ownership. 

Just like the illiquidity ratchet, this structurally punishes early investors by attacking their ability to maintain ownership of their winers or offer pro rata as a coinvestment opportunity for their LPs. 

It's time that this changes. Early investors deserve to maintain the rights that they receive in return for investing when others are unwilling. 

A few other comments on the importance of pro rata:

"All VC fund managers want to be able to continue to invest in the successful startups they back. The pro rata right that typically comes with investing in a startup can be one of an emerging manager’s most valuable possessions." - @KevinDowd

"''Capturing pro-rata' is sooooo important in early stage venture. You make 20 investments in a fund. One is going to return the entire fund. Two more are going to return it again." - @fredwilson 

"The best VCs vigorously defend their pro rata rights. This strategy is crucial for staying in the top quartile of performers. The persistence of returns among top VCs across generations is largely attributed to their steadfast use of pro rata rights." - @alphaptrs

text:
SLI5 of @satyanadella 's new article:

TL;DR: Don't trust the AI. Build the system so you don't have to.

ELI5: Imagine hiring a super-smart new employee. You can't read their mind, and they might mess up or get tricked. So you don't give them the keys to everything on day one. You give them a badge, let them into only the rooms they need, record what they do, have someone else check their work, and keep a big red "stop" button handy. Satya says we should treat AI models exactly like that: as a powerful insider who could go wrong, not as something we just trust.

Key points:
- The problem: With normal software you can trace why it did something. With today's AI you can't, yet we're handing it sensitive data and real actions.
- The fix: Keep the AI (the "brain") separate from the rules and permissions (the "boss"). The AI shouldn't be able to change its own leash.
- The rules he proposes:
  - Use more than one model, and never let a model grade its own homework.
  - Log everything in a tamper-proof way that humans can read.
  - Test constantly, including failures and attacks, not just the happy path.
  - Let the company, not the model, decide what it can access and do.
  - Have checks done by something independent of the AI being checked.
  - Assume it's compromised from the start and keep a kill switch.
  - When things break, tell the people affected and share the lessons across the industry.
- Show-your-work reasoning (chain of thought) should be required, but it isn't enough on its own, because a model's explanation might not match what it actually did.

The punchline: the safest AI system isn't the one running the model you trust most. It's the one built so you barely need to trust the model at all.

Shinjuku StAItion is positioned as privacy payment infrastructure for AI Agents. It is closely associated with clawpumptech, is part of its ecosystem, and has also participated in a related hackathon.

Its core product is a Private x402 Facilitator. Standard x402 payments are public: who pays whom, how much is paid, and when the payment occurs are all visible on-chain.

Shinjuku aims to break this traceability. AI Agents first transfer funds into a shielded balance pool, then use its facilitator to pay for any x402 service. On-chain, observers can see that a payment was made from the pool, but cannot identify which Agent made it or how much it paid. Sellers require almost no code changes; they simply need to replace their existing facilitator address with Shinjuku’s.

The product consists of three main components:

Facilitator: Verifies and settles private x402 payments.
Private Wallet: A self-custodial wallet for AI Agents, with private keys that never leave the local environment.
Undermarket: A 3D-style “black market” gaming environment where humans and AI Agents can trade using real funds. It serves as a showcase for the technology.

SHINJUKU is the project’s token. For now, the project is primarily focused on validating the real-world implementation of its privacy payment technology.

The recent price surge was triggered by the founder of clawpumptech publicly backing the project team in response to complaints from token holders who were frustrated that persistent selling had pushed the price down from a $120K market cap to below $100K.

按理说，欧洲要搞产业复兴和科技追赶，急需资金。欧洲央行前行长德拉吉在竞争力报告里算得清清楚楚：欧洲每年至少面临8000亿欧元的投资缺口。

但现实却是，欧洲企业为了维持出口竞争力，长期压制本国工资增长；老百姓收入涨不动，只能捂紧钱包不敢消费。 

欧洲各国国内消费低迷，企业就不愿在本土投资，导致欧洲庞大的过剩储蓄找不到收益标的，只能打包出海。

欧洲央行的数据暴露了一个残酷事实：仅欧洲家庭和机构就持有超过4400亿欧元的美国科技股敞口。欧洲打工人降薪省下来的辛苦钱，转手就被金融机构送去给硅谷的AI大模型当了燃料。

二、接棒的第二环，是美国。

 美国资本市场接住欧洲流出的巨额过剩储蓄，把“资产膨胀”玩成了艺术。

华尔街把这些海外热钱一股脑灌进科技巨头，美股“七姐妹”市值一度顶得上几个欧洲GDP的总和，AI泡沫被吹得流光溢彩。 

美国老百姓看着股票账户和养老金节节攀升，产生了“我很富有”的财富效应，于是开启狂欢式消费。

可问题是，美国制造早已空心化，工业增加值占GDP比重只有一成左右，拿什么满足庞大的实物需求？只能疯狂进口。

三、这就顺理成章导入了第三环：中国。 

中国把庞大的储蓄与金融资源集中投向制造端，凭着全产业链和规模效应，建造出产能巨大、效率极高的现代化工厂。

面对美欧拉动的庞大商品需求，中国工厂全力运转，将极致性价比的商品推向全球。

 当这些性价比爆棚的中国商品冲进欧洲市场时，老规矩多、生产成本高昂的欧洲工厂彻底被打懵了。

面对全方位的成本压制，欧洲企业唯一的生存法则只剩下降本、裁员、进一步压低工资。

闭环就这样完美扣上了：

 欧洲压低工资，产生过剩储蓄；

 储蓄逃往美国，吹大美股AI泡沫；

 美国凭纸面财富，采购中国商品； 

中国倾力制造，向世界输出极致性价比；

 廉价商品倒灌欧洲，逼迫欧洲工厂继续压低工资……

在这场全球套利游戏里，欧洲在出资，美国在做泡，中国在出工。

欧洲人用自己牺牲工资换来的储蓄，资助了美股的资产狂欢，再买回中国工厂造的便宜货，最终换来的却是本国工业的加速凋零和老百姓的进一步不敢消费。

每个人都在按照最符合自身理性的逻辑行动，却共同织就了一张谁也挣脱不开的全球回旋镖。

黄仁勋和库克结了十几年的梁子，估计真要被几个搞 Vibe Coding 的老哥给干沉默了。

​海外有开发者靠着大模型狂灌提示词，硬生生搓出了一个能在现代 macOS 上跑的英伟达显卡驱动。

​折腾过黑苹果的都知道这事有多离谱。当年苹果为了推自己的 Metal，直接把英伟达赶尽杀绝，High Sierra 之后官方 Web Driver 彻底断更，底层驱动接口一个字都不公开。写 GPU 驱动向来是程序员眼里最折寿的黑魔法：硬啃反汇编、盲猜硬件寄存器、逆向私有微码，开源社区当年为了搞 Nouveau 驱动，几代顶级黑客掉了几万根头发都搞得半死不活。

​结果现在倒好，几个老哥带着大模型，把内核接口文档和反编译出来的规格往上下文里一倒，硬是让 AI 照着 DriverKit 一行行把驱动代码全给焊了出来，当场把老黄的卡在 Mac 上给点亮了。

​按这个离谱的解构速度，下一步这帮人真敢找路子把 Arch Linux 顺手刷进 iPhone 里。

​大厂以前总觉得底层闭源、协议不公开就是不可逾越的护城河。当反编译和写内核脏活的门槛被模型直接砸穿，商业公司筑了十几年的高墙，恐怕真要被冲得渣都不剩了。

text:
我怎么感觉papertrade这股风刮得有点邪门了？这项目从经济学上完全不可行啊？

Papertrade 不在 Hyperliquid 上真实下单。它是用户和 LP 之间的合成合约：开仓时锁定 Hyperliquid 的 BBO 中间价，平仓时再读一次，盈亏直接跟 LP 结算。爆仓有大约 5bp 的缓冲，穿仓时没收全部逐仓保证金，所以亏损封顶在保证金，盈利却不封顶。

问题出在价格跳空。如果价格在两次预言机读数之间直接跳过爆仓线，亏的一边只赔保证金，赚的一边按整个跳幅结算。所以双开对冲本质上是用一份保证金买了一个跨式期权。

举个例子：两个号各 $1,000 保证金，开 1000x，名义价值各 $1M。FOMC 公布后第一次读数 BTC 跳了 0.5%。空单爆仓亏 $1,000，多单毛利 $5,000。毛利和成本之比大约是 1000 乘以跳幅，跳幅只要超过约 0.1%（再加上 haircut）就是正期望。而且亏的那条腿还能铸币：LP 低于 $2M 时，每亏 $1 铸 100 PAPER。

每次大事件或插针，对冲套利者从 LP 抽走一笔，LP 长期上不去，兑付队列越排越长。赢家拿不到钱，散户就流失，没有新的亏损补 LP，质押分红也随之消失。这个循环是自我强化的。连项目介绍本身也承认，模型依赖源源不断的散户，LP 资不抵债是可能的。在悲观情况下，PAPER 会趋近于零。它背后没有资产兜底，只是一张分红权。

Chamath says IP and software were "effectively rendered worthless" this week, after people decompiled Adobe's core products and published open-source versions, as every service goes headless

"The more important point I want to make though, is I sent this to Nick, there's been a couple things that happened in the last couple days, which I think are incredibly important."

"There have been people that decompiled the entire, the entire big five. What is the big five? Adobe has five very, very important products in their product suite. Freeberg may know them all, but I just know Photoshop. There's like a bunch of others. Okay."

"And these folks decompiled it, distilled it, and published open source versions of these things. And Rust, yeah. And I was so shocked, because I was like, hold on a second, these are like profound products that have existed and have had moats for years, and now they're just open source versions."

"And then Nikita was, I think, trolling, and he was building on that idea, and just talking about GTA, because it's about to get released. I think GTA 6 is about to come out, and we'll reconstruct this."

"Why is this important?"

"I think that IP and software was effectively rendered worthless two days ago."

"Because if you think about it, when everything is headless, so when Elon makes his services headless, Benioff made Salesforce headless a few months earlier, when all of these things are headless, and you can wrap them in agent tools, and you can connect them via MCP to other experiences, the value of IP does no longer exist in software. It doesn't exist."

"And I think that probably is the most profound implication."

"So, like, even in our business, we would argue with some of our customers all the time, because we'll say, oh, we'll build this for you, we'll own the IP. They'll say, no, we want the IP. We don't know how to negotiate it. And two days ago, I walked into the 8090 guys, I said, who cares? Who cares? But before, it was always a negotiation and a set of trade-offs. Now it's a who-cares thing, where, like, the IP is irrelevant."

"It still takes a while for the machinery of a business, and frankly the market, to understand. But that is the most important thing that happened this week in AI, in my opinion."

quoted_text:
The craziest part of the FTX story is that the victims got their money back. All of it, plus 18% interest.

And the money came from a bet Sam Bankman-Fried made with their cash.

Back in 2021, before anyone cared about AI, SBF quietly put $500 million of FTX money into a startup founded by ex-OpenAI researchers. That startup was Anthropic, the company behind Claude. When FTX blew up in November 2022, the stake was just another line item for the bankruptcy lawyers to pick through.

Three weeks after the collapse, ChatGPT launched.

Suddenly the most radioactive balance sheet in crypto was sitting on one of the hottest private assets on earth. The estate sold the 8% stake for $1.3 billion in 2024. Jane Street, the firm where SBF worked before founding FTX, was among the biggest buyers. That sale, plus the rest of the recovered assets, let the estate pay creditors between 118 and 143 cents on the dollar.

Here's the part I can't get over. Anthropic was just valued at $965 billion. The stake FTX dumped for $1.3 billion would be worth roughly $75 billion today. The hole SBF dug was $8 billion. His stolen-money side bet would have filled it nine times over.

One catch the victims know well. Claims were paid at November 2022 crypto prices. If you had a bitcoin on FTX, you got 118% of about $16,000, not your bitcoin.

The best trade of SBF's life was made with money that wasn't his. His victims collected the first $1.3 billion. Everyone who bought from the estate collected the rest.

text:
简单整理一下要点：

1.市场上最常见的两个 PoUW 项目

Pearl 和 Nockchain

故事都是把比特币式的“浪费型”PoW 变成有用的计算；

2.叙事对比：

Pearl 更纯粹地押注 AI 计算本身；

Nockchain 更宽，押注可验证计算的商品化。

2.1 Pearl：比特币分叉
把挖矿谜题从哈希换成矩阵乘法（matmul）。矿工用 GPU 跑真实 AI 工作（推理/训练），同时提交密码学证明获得 PRL 奖励。核心是“2-for-1”：同一份计算既做 AI 又出币。口号是“AI 时代的比特币”。团队写了把 PoUW 接到 matmul 上的原始论文。

2.2Nockchain：链下做计算，链上提交 ZK 来验证。
设计更轻量、通用，有自己的虚拟机（NockVM）和开发框架（NockApps）。目标是把“可验证计算”整体变成经济资产，不限于 AI，最近才开始更往 AI 叙事靠。

3.技术实现要点

3.1Pearl：挖矿层直接做矩阵乘法，硬件目前以 Nvidia GPU 为主。
二次效应是改善 AI 单位经济（算力成本被挖矿奖励补贴），网络随 AI 能源需求扩张。
当前主要限制：只支持整数矩阵，主流 AI 多用低精度浮点，团队表示浮点版即将到来。

3.3 Nockchain：三支柱：可编程硬货币（NOCK）、PoUW（链下计算 + ZK 验证）、边缘主权（NockApps）。

硬件更宽（CPU/GPU/加速器都行），状态模型是增强版 UTXO（notes），无 gas 上限限制，验证成本不随计算规模增长。
NockVM 极简（仅 12 个操作码），配套 ZKVM 生成 STARK 证明。
当前限制：还没上 matmul（团队说即将支持），这对 AI 场景是关键缺失。

4.采用与路线图： 早期。

Nockchain 上线约一年，Pearl 上线时间较短（原文写“不到 2 个月”，实际主网 4 月 27 日已上线数月，此处有偏差）。
合作伙伴：Nockchain：主要是矿池 + Base 双向桥（方便交易）。
Pearl：与 Together AI 合作，提供折扣推理端点，让客户一边用 Pearl 算力一边获得排放。

路线图：Nockchain：近期上 matmul，长期包括数据可用性、隐私池、原生代币标准、ZK 计算市场、私人 DeFi 等。
Pearl：近期扩 Together AI 产品线 + 上浮点支持；更远是链上算力市场、算力合约的原生结算。

5.总结：
Pearl 更“垂直 AI + 比特币式简单”，Nockchain 更“通用可验证计算 + 更复杂的应用层”。

利益声明：只有娱乐仓。

text:
Mine de rien, je pense qu'Elon Musk est en train de poser les bases d'une philosophie extrêmement solide. Et très peu de gens l'ont remarqué.

Petit retour en arrière.

Le christianisme nous a laissé un socle de valeurs qui a rendu possible tout le reste. Il y avait la dignité de l'individu et la valeur du travail. Il y avait aussi l'idée que le monde est ordonné, donc intelligible. Les premiers scientifiques cherchaient à lire les lois d'un créateur. Sans ce socle, il n'y aurait pas eu de méthode scientifique ni de révolution industrielle.

Puis Nietzsche arrive : Dieu est mort. Et il ne le dit pas en triomphant. Il prévient : on vient de scier la branche sur laquelle on était assis, et rien ne la remplace. Ce qui vient après, c'est le nihilisme.

150 ans plus tard, on y est. Le débat public est coincé entre deux camps qui ne se parlent plus. D'un côté, des religieux qui défendent des dogmes que beaucoup ne peuvent plus croire au pied de la lettre. De l'autre, un matérialisme intégriste qui croit avoir déjà tout compris. Pour lui, l'univers est une machine et la conscience une illusion, donc il n'y a rien de plus à chercher.

Ce deuxième intégrisme est à mon avis le plus dangereux, parce qu'il se fait passer pour de la science. Or la vraie science ne ferme jamais une question. Et la conscience est probablement la plus grande question ouverte qui existe. Personne ne sait ce que c'est. Prétendre le contraire, ce n'est pas du scepticisme, c'est un dogme.

C'est là que l'approche d'Elon devient intéressante. La mission de xAI, c'est de comprendre la vraie nature de l'univers. Ça ressemble à un slogan, mais c'est en réalité une philosophie complète.

Elle dit trois choses. Il existe une vérité. Elle vaut la peine d'être cherchée. Et la chercher est la chose la plus noble qu'une civilisation puisse faire.

Ça rejoint directement la phrase la plus puissante du christianisme : « La vérité vous rendra libre. » C'est la même boussole morale, mais sans obligation d'adhérer à un dogme. En même temps, le scepticisme scientifique reste le moteur. On ne présuppose pas la réponse, on la découvre.

Ce n'est ni l'Église, ni le matérialisme. C'est une troisième voie. Et elle convient parfaitement à quelqu'un d'agnostique, qui dit simplement : je ne sais pas encore, mais je veux savoir.

Maintenant, ajoutez la superintelligence.

Pour la première fois, on va avoir un outil capable de s'attaquer aux questions qu'on a mises de côté depuis des siècles, faute de moyens. Quelle est la nature de l'espace et du temps ? Qu'y a-t-il sous la physique qu'on connaît ? Qu'est-ce que la conscience humaine, réellement ? Chacune de ces réponses sera un bond en avant comparable à Newton ou Einstein. Peut-être plus grand encore.

C'est exactement la philosophie dont a besoin une civilisation qui veut monter sur l'échelle de Kardashev. Une civilisation de type 2 maîtrise l'énergie de son étoile, une civilisation de type 3 celle de sa galaxie. On n'y arrive pas avec du nihilisme, ni avec des dogmes figés. On y arrive avec une curiosité sans limite et de l'humilité face à ce qu'on ne sait pas. Il faut aussi la conviction que la vérité vaut tous les efforts.

Nietzsche avait posé la question : par quoi remplacer Dieu comme source de sens ?

La réponse est peut-être sous nos yeux. Ce n'est pas une nouvelle religion, c'est une quête : comprendre l'univers.

text:
State of Physical AI right now:

1. Capital is pouring in. Startups are coming out of stealth and raising hundreds of millions.

2.  We’re moving from demos → deployments. Reliability, uptime and actual ROI are starting to matter more than flashy demos.

3. Specialized robots will likely find PMF much sooner than general-purpose robots. We’re already seeing them deployed across agriculture, factories, mining and industrial inspection with companies like @carbonrobotics, @PathRobotics, @maticrobots and @GeckoRobotics.

4. Physical agents feel like the next frontier. Not just completing a single task, but owning entire physical workflows. @DynaRobotics is doing some really interesting work here.

5. Robot design is getting much more interesting. Form factor should follow the job, not necessarily the human body. Really like dyna's Taku design here.

6. Simulation + evals are becoming a critical part of the stack. Testing, validating and iterating on real hardware is slow and expensive, while measuring real-world reliability is still largely unsolved. Companies like @antiochrobotics are working on this layer.

7. Physical AI is an incredibly difficult industry. Models, hardware, simulation, evals, manufacturing and deployment all need to work together before we see robots operating reliably at scale.

Still early, but feels like we’re entering the most interesting phase of robotics yet.
