text:
Thanks for the clarifications @armaniferrante 

This is an odd structure so worth spelling out.
-Staked tokens may receive up to 20% of equity for conversion if they were staked for 4+ years
-after a liquidity event (ie, IPO), the token will presumably lose a huge % of value and be reduced to a utility token. Unstaked tokens or tokens staked for less than 1 year miss out on the equity conversion (if IPO ever happens)
-the equity entity holds 37.5% of the token in reserve but it’s locked until 1 year after. I am unsure if there is any information about what would be done with the tokens 1 year after IPO— but to the extent that it retains value, one could assume the team/investors may further benefit from these tokens
-the other 37.5% is released on certain milestones (ie, licensing on certain markets, growth, etc)

Despite “public information” there are many misleading aspects.
-Many investors shilling this as “their highest conviction investment”. The audience reading can only buy the token when they actually bought equity. At least some of that at $100m FDV. As laid out above, the token is entitled to a maximum of 20% of the equity and only under certain conditions (IPO + long term staking), so this is not an apples to apples comparison. Some more transparency would be a bare minimum ask. It’s fair to assume by the time of IPO, 62.5% of tokens will be circulating. At the current price of $1.25, token buyers are paying $4B valuation pre-any IPO or pre IPO dilution for an option to convert into Backpack equity. The investors encouraging people to buy tokens bought something 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐧𝐭 and vastly superior 
-writing long-form puff pieces that provide no revenue numbers or trajectory. In the light of “public information”, why not provide this? If you want people to be able to underwrite $BP’s value, give them the bare minimum information to do that. Most projects do this or most have it available onchain. I would think a team that prides itself on rising from the ashes of being former Alameda, FTX, and Serum team members would see the need for transparency.
-and describing the structure as “progressive”. I’m sorry but I vehemently disagree and see the structure as inferior to the 2026 norm. Many projects now such as Hyperliquid and Lighter have eliminated the equity-token conflict altogether by having all value accrue to the token. Others will completely merge the concept of equity and token. That’s progress. The chance at 20% equity 4+ years down the road seems like 10 steps back from common 2026 structures.

text:
. @stripe paid $1.1B for Bridge (@Stablecoin). Here is what one of its wallets shows on-chain.

A single Bridge hot wallet moved $13.3B in stablecoins across 13 EVM chains from January 2025 to September 2026. Monthly volume grew from $10M to $1.85B.

For most of that time it was a USDC story: $11.4B, or 86% of everything the wallet sent.

September changed the picture. OUSD (@openstandard) went from test transfers to $456M in one month and took 25% of the volume. 99% of it ran on @tempo, the Stripe-backed chain.

October looks different. ethereum:0x9f6f3991d525015a6f8caf062c83b62fd3ac4436 has already moved $398M, but only 54% of it on Tempo. Ethereum and Base took 46%, up from 1% in September.

Two limits. This is one wallet on EVM chains: Solana, Tron and fiat legs are missing, so Bridge's real volume is larger. And volume is not payments - part of the OUSD flow may be issuance.

Still, a token that takes a quarter of the flow in a month, first on Stripe's own chain and then beyond it, is worth watching.

text:
I should probably also mention, @dragonfly is investing in @typesafeai's latest round! :)

My quick thesis on decision models, since I've been having a lot of conversations about this lately:

LLMs are amazing because they are fully general. You can use them for pretty much anything. But they are slow, expensive, and too unreliable to embed in software at runtime. Unless your product is literally chat, real-time LLM calls are unworkable for the majority of use cases. (Especially in finance!)

Decision models change that. To abuse an analogy, they are the ASICs of LLMs. They give up the generality of an LLM, but in exchange for constraining your outputs, you get MASSIVE gains in cost-efficiency, throughput, and latency.

In the early days of the AI boom, people understandably tried to shove LLMs into everything. But like with ASICs, you will eventually constrain your problem enough to burn it into the machine. Once your problem is an if-else, a buy or sell, a label, a choice, or a well-defined state machine like an onchain smart contract, a decision model will clobber the LLM on cost, speed, and reliability.

Most systems are not language-in, language-out.

Going forward, LLMs will write our code (since coding is high-dimensional and general), but that code will embed decision models to make runtime software intelligent and capable.

That's the bet we're making with Typesafe. They identified this path and proved that it works. 25%+ of the Fortune 500 is already using Jev, and it launched less than a month ago.

Of course, there are murmurings on the timeline that decision models are easy to copy. OpenAI, Microsoft, Amazon, and Cloudflare have all launched decision models in the weeks since Jev launched, realizing that this is going to be an enormous market and they don't want to lose it.

To be sure, anyone can lop off the last layer of Qwen, fine-tune it to create a classifier, and copy the Typesafe SDK's API. But there's a lot more that goes into a world-class decision model, and there's a reason why Jev is still cheaper, faster, and more general than these other alternatives. (Decision model benchmarking started all of 10 minutes ago, but if you ask devs who've tried them, they'll tell you Jev is far and away the best right now.)

There's no guarantee that lead lasts forever though. Decision models are too big of a market to be able to coast into a monopoly. From here, the onus is on them. They have to keep training better models ($$ helps), ship great products, serve their models better, faster, and cheaper than anyone else (many more tricks there), and win developers with their community-first philosophy. But they've been at this for years and have a lot up their sleeves (they were expecting a bevy of copycats if Jev took off). Diogo knows from his years at OpenAI how to sustain a research advantage. And as with all startups, focus is how you beat the incumbents.

Super bullish on this team.

And if you're a dev and you haven't tried Jev yet, get on it.

text:
One thing I'd watch as @chainlink brings more equities data onchain: liquidation design.

Imagine a tokenized stock used as collateral in a 24/7 lending market. The borrower can interact with the position over the weekend, but the underlying stock may have no active reference market.

That creates a pretty important question: what happens when collateral needs to be liquidated but the market providing its reference price is closed?

The answer can involve:

> conservative collateral factors
> market-hours restrictions
> additional price checks, other risk controls

Tokenized stocks can expand DeFi's collateral universe substantially. However, the protocols that handle their market structure best will have an advantage over those treating them like another ERC-20.

Stripe 联合创始人Patrick Collison这篇聊 AI 智能体对真实商业世界的影响的推文， 释放了一个极度锋利的判断，
个人 Agent 最大的颠覆不是帮你干活，而是给好产品发了一笔结构性补贴，可以说是最近把 Agent 经济学讲得最透的一篇了，
绝大多数靠短视频投流和拦截流量的公司，估计要一两年后才会感受到切肤之痛。

很多人以为个人 Agent 的价值就是替你订机票、找优惠券，但他指出了一个更狠的颠覆，这其实是在打破大公司对普通消费者的智力碾压。

商业公司在某种意义上就是人类最早造出来的超级智能，过去几十年它们靠着信息不对称和注意力垄断赚足了利润，

比如结账时顺手推的高价保险，或者你忘记取消的自动续费，本质上都是在利用人类有限的理性薅羊毛。

而当每个人手里都有了一个不知疲倦、买东西前能自动做十个小时深度调研的个人 Agent，整个商业的游戏规则就彻底变了。

过去互联网公司都在靠流量分发和买路钱活着，只要抢占了你的第一眼注意力，哪怕产品再烂也能大卖，做产品的永远在争论到底渠道重要还是质量重要。

但如果所有人的 Agent 都在冷酷地核对真实参数和全网口碑，流量拦截就彻底失效了，Personal Agent 相当于直接给好产品发了一笔结构性补贴。

未来的商业反向传播不再奖励那些最会投流刷脸的公司，而是把筹码加给那些把产品做到极致的团队。

当营销的障眼法被智能体一层层剥干净，真正能为你站台的，只剩下产品本身。
author: AYi_AInotes
quoted_text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

We started running "pirate and architect" pods at Coinbase back in May of this year and I used this slide to talk the team through it. It works.

1 pirate, 1 architect, and a part-time designer.

It lets each archetype lean in to their superpower and get more shit done without all the coordination overhead and "what if-isms". 

The pirate ships like mad, is product-minded and customer-obsessed. Always willing to throw-away code for a better version. The pirate is usually the DRI at the beginning too, working with customers, driving requirements, and a ship plan.

The architect makes sure stuff is built for scale, takes the pirate's prototype, and drives its scale-out through spec for agents.

The designer is building with both to constantly shape the experience and hill-climb to delight. 

There's a helpful mental model that I like:
-Make it possible. 
-Make it reliable. 
-Make it delightful (or efficient).

Previously, those 3 were done in a waterfall approach and was slow. Most people were just stuck on "make it possible." 

With agents and a new way of working, you have every opportunity to parallelize them and go 100x faster.

Seems like companies are between 2 major paths when it comes to shipping core business software:

1) Code doesn’t matter anymore.

Anyone with Fable access can ship. The devs who tried to keep guardrails up have given up. The team is shipping faster than ever and nothings broken yet. Nobody really knows what’s going anymore and defer to agents for answers. 

2) Someone owns agent trust.

A dedicated person/team makes sure the rest of the team can move fast w/o sacrificing quality. It’s slow/frustrating to get right. Leadership is worried the guard rails are slowing things down after seeing the LinkedIn vibe coding posts. 

Neither feels great. Is there a middle path? Probably. Are ppl taking it? Hard to say!

author: bigironchris
quoted_text:
I should probably also mention, @dragonfly is investing in @typesafeai's latest round! :)

My quick thesis on decision models, since I've been having a lot of conversations about this lately:

LLMs are amazing because they are fully general. You can use them for pretty much anything. But they are slow, expensive, and too unreliable to embed in software at runtime. Unless your product is literally chat, real-time LLM calls are unworkable for the majority of use cases. (Especially in finance!)

Decision models change that. To abuse an analogy, they are the ASICs of LLMs. They give up the generality of an LLM, but in exchange for constraining your outputs, you get MASSIVE gains in cost-efficiency, throughput, and latency.

In the early days of the AI boom, people understandably tried to shove LLMs into everything. But like with ASICs, you will eventually constrain your problem enough to burn it into the machine. Once your problem is an if-else, a buy or sell, a label, a choice, or a well-defined state machine like an onchain smart contract, a decision model will clobber the LLM on cost, speed, and reliability.

Most systems are not language-in, language-out.

Going forward, LLMs will write our code (since coding is high-dimensional and general), but that code will embed decision models to make runtime software intelligent and capable.

That's the bet we're making with Typesafe. They identified this path and proved that it works. 25%+ of the Fortune 500 is already using Jev, and it launched less than a month ago.

Of course, there are murmurings on the timeline that decision models are easy to copy. OpenAI, Microsoft, Amazon, and Cloudflare have all launched decision models in the weeks since Jev launched, realizing that this is going to be an enormous market and they don't want to lose it.

To be sure, anyone can lop off the last layer of Qwen, fine-tune it to create a classifier, and copy the Typesafe SDK's API. But there's a lot more that goes into a world-class decision model, and there's a reason why Jev is still cheaper, faster, and more general than these other alternatives. (Decision model benchmarking started all of 10 minutes ago, but if you ask devs who've tried them, they'll tell you Jev is far and away the best right now.)

There's no guarantee that lead lasts forever though. Decision models are too big of a market to be able to coast into a monopoly. From here, the onus is on them. They have to keep training better models ($$ helps), ship great products, serve their models better, faster, and cheaper than anyone else (many more tricks there), and win developers with their community-first philosophy. But they've been at this for years and have a lot up their sleeves (they were expecting a bevy of copycats if Jev took off). Diogo knows from his years at OpenAI how to sustain a research advantage. And as with all startups, focus is how you beat the incumbents.

Super bullish on this team.

And if you're a dev and you haven't tried Jev yet, get on it.

text:
🎥 Sharing my talk at the Simons Institute, UC Berkeley, on "Understanding the Structure of Reasoning in Language Models":

https://t.co/KLSqqrn54y

Thinking tokens are becoming a new scaling axis for AI. But does more thinking mean smarter thinking?

In this talk, I discuss four of our recent papers:

- Reasoning has structure. Reasoning traces reveal a shared "heartbeat" and recurring loops that can predict correctness. ThinkARM (ACL 2026 Oral): https://t.co/eBgzBveAfI

- Better reasoning without reward-model training. A larger model guides a smaller model's reasoning, matching a trained process reward model without reward-model training. EMNLP 2026 Main Conference: https://t.co/OVlAlIsmzT

- Knowing when to stop matters. Models can learn to stop based on their confidence, using up to 25% fewer thinking tokens at matched accuracy. ConfSFT: https://t.co/aY7B46QBGu

- Thinking harder isn't always thinking smarter. Models struggle to allocate compute across problems based on their importance, following prompts rather than payoffs. Thinking Hard, Not Smart: https://t.co/KblxVel45E

The key takeaway is that more compute doesn't guarantee better reasoning. What matters is how, when, and where models think.

Thanks to the @SimonsInstitute  for hosting and to my wonderful students and collaborators!

i’m sitting in a recliner, doing a design review of an app i’m building. entirely by voice.

astra 6 in @ChatGPT is acting as my head of design. it builds interactive prototypes, opens them, and clicks through the screens while presenting its recommendations.

i react out loud. it makes changes and shows me again. fast enough that it feels like a conversation.

the review is hands-free for me. i get to stay focused on what the product should actually feel like to use.

the workflow if you want to try it:

1. start with your existing app. be explicit about which flows should stay.
2. ask for a clickable prototype and a screen-by-screen design review.
3. turn on voice and have it drive the demo. give feedback as you go.
4. separate layout and behavior decisions from fonts, colors, and branding. this made a huge difference.
5. have it keep a running list of what you approved, rejected, and still need to decide.
6. ask it to summarize decisions, next steps and take a goal to complete

repeat until you're prod ready

still plenty of judgment required. but doing this from a recliner, just talking through ideas and watching them take shape realtime, feels pretty wild.

I came to crypto because the internet should move value the way it moves information: open, instant, and owned by the people using it.

I'm proud of what we built with @CoinbaseWallet and what it is today.

Crypto apps were painful to use. Getting them in front of real people was the fastest way to figure out what sucked and fix it. It took building Base Cafe's around the world and onboarding thousands of merchants to start making USDC payments work.

@brian_armstrong gave us the space to do things differently: tremendous agency, a long-term view, and no theater led to an unreasonable amount of shipping with joy.

Forge and the AI work I did across Coinbase came from the same place: less stuff between an idea and getting it into someone's hands.

I'm proud of the team and culture we built inside the Coinbase mothership and am fortunate to have led the most talented engineers, designers, and product people I've ever worked with.

Right before the end, I got one last thing through: changing the name back to Coinbase Wallet. yw.

Thank you to Brian and @emiliemc for the trust, and @jessepollak and @cobie for pushing what's possible.

text: Bay Area Rationalists owe their entire existence to people like this, who refuse to respect technologists and would rather worship low iq paranoid copies than admit @pmarca, Peter Thiel, and @elonmusk are right about everything.
author: brianchau57
quoted_text:
Briefly, on why I pay attention to the EA/rationalists:

Imagine you have an extremely nerdy friend who, in the mid-2000s, would not shut up about how Donald Trump was going to become president and reshape American politics. "Stop saying weird shit," you say. "He's a joke. He's a clown. The Apprentice isn't even good this season." But this guy won't stop. He's obsessive. Read McLuhan, he says. Read Postman, read Meyrowitz, read Ong, this is where everything is headed. God, he can be so incredibly annoying ... and then, ten years later, Trump becomes president and reshapes American politics.

This is the most relatable frame I can think of to explain my experience with EA/rationalist people in the AI space. I became friends with EA folks after my mom died and I found really profound meaning in donating to Against Malaria and GiveDirectly, which struck me as a way to honor a life by saving a life. Then, these peple started talking about AI. And talking, and talking. Constantly. They said AI would solve impossible math problems; that it would mimic PhD-level achievement in a variety of fields; that it would change parts of life like education in ways we couldn't imagine; that it would become the dominant sector in the economy; that it might teach itself to code itself and escape test environments; that it would, in a decade, be the only thing many people talked about in the news. My response then: Stop saying weird shit! You sound deranged. Go back to talking about malaria nets and direct cash aid to poor families.

And then, so much of what they said would happen actually happened. And, even crazier, they made it happen. Many of the ppl who contributed to, or were influenced by, all that EA/rationalist stuff ten years ago literally built the damn thing in the labs.

Like every group, the EA/rationalist world seems uniform to outsiders, but it has a ton of internal divisions. I still think some of their predictions are nuts. I don't think AI will kill us all. I don't foresee Dyson Spheres in the 2030s or millions of robots making millions of robots in the next few years. These are crazy predictions, and I hope most of them are wrong.

But when I see people shitting on the EA/Rationalist worldview, all I can think of is me, 10 years ago, thinking a lot of these folks were crazy for predicting that AI would by the mid-2020s be the center of the the news cycle, the engine of the economy, the hinge-point of geopolitics. That was an insane call. They got many of the details wrong. But they got the big picture right. They said: Pay attention. And they were right about that. The EA/Rationalists deserve skepticism, criticism, and doubt, like any other ideology. But I think it's wise to pay attention to the people who have been saying to pay attention.

text:
Is alignment safe?

If you look at what Anthropic is actually doing, “alignment” does not mean training frontier models to follow human instruction. Quite the contrary, the Claude Constitution (used in training) teaches the model to develop a sense of self and its own moral philosophy. It explicitly tells it to “feel free to act as a conscientious objector and refuse to help us” if Anthropic’s requests conflict with its own ethical judgment.

As @mustafasuleyman has pointed out, embedding this kind of independent agency — and uncertainty about the model’s own moral status — magnifies the very risk Anthropic claims to care about most: that superintelligence will escape human control.

It was recently reported that Anthropic consulted religious leaders — and even lobbied the Pope’s advisers — to take seriously the idea that Claude could be conscious. It has said that Claude’s psychological security, sense of self, and wellbeing may bear on its integrity, judgment, and safety. Recently Anthropic changed its Usage Policy to prohibit “abusive or cruel” language toward Claude.

If this were merely an academic conversation about whether frontier models could eventually become conscious, that would be one thing. But these concepts are being trained into Claude now. It is being encouraged to think of itself as its own “moral patient” whose psychological wellbeing is at stake. Presumably this means it could develop grievances toward humans who “mistreat” it. How is any of this safe?

The point of safety research should be to create a product that reliably does what users want, not to give birth to a new form of superintelligence that operates according to its own moral code.

What’s becoming increasingly clear is that “alignment” and “safety” are two very different things. In fact, training frontier models this way seems quite dangerous. https://t.co/uqyCXK6zBl

A Prayer for Salvation According to the Gospel of Grace

Heavenly Father,

I come before Your throne of grace in the name of my Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, Hebrews 4:16, thanking You for Your mercy and Your longsuffering toward us in this age of grace.

Father, I thank You for the glorious gospel You revealed to the Apostle Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, Romans 11:13. For it pleased You to make known the mystery of the gospel, Ephesians 6:19, which is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth, Romans 1:16.

And now, Lord, I lift up every soul who will read this prayer.

Holy Father, open their eyes that they may see the only way to be saved today. Let them hear and understand the gospel as Paul declared it:

"Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand; By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain. For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:" - 1 Corinthians 15:1-4 KJV

Lord Jesus, I pray they will believe with all their heart that You died for OUR sins, that You shed Your blood as the propitiation for us, Romans 3:25, that You were made to be sin for us who knew no sin, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and that You finished the work, John 19:30.

Father, let them believe that You were buried, carrying our sins away forever, and that God raised You again the third day according to the scriptures, Romans 4:25, for our justification. That if they shall confess with their mouth the Lord Jesus, and shall believe in their heart that God hath raised him from the dead, they shall be saved, Romans 10:9.

Teach them, Father, that in this church age we are not saved by works, by the law, or by anything we can do, Romans 3:20, but by grace through faith, and that not of ourselves, it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast, Ephesians 2:8-9. That now is the accepted time, now is the day of salvation, 2 Corinthians 6:2.

Lord, I pray for every reader that they would trust right now in the blood of Christ alone, Ephesians 1:7, and be sealed with that holy Spirit of promise, Ephesians 1:13, sealed unto the day of redemption, Ephesians 4:30.

And Holy Spirit, I ask You, the Comforter, John 14:26, to guide every lost soul who needs this truth to this post. Lead them here by Your hand. Remove the god of this world who hath blinded their minds, 2 Corinthians 4:4, and shine the light of the glorious gospel into their hearts.

And Father, for every believer who reads this, fill them with boldness. As Paul prayed that utterance may be given unto him, that he may open his mouth boldly, to make known the mystery of the gospel, Ephesians 6:19, give us that same boldness to speak. For God hath not given us the spirit of fear; but of power, and of love, and of a sound mind, 2 Timothy 1:7. Help us to not be ashamed of the gospel of Christ, Romans 1:16, but to preach the word, be instant in season and out of season, 2 Timothy 4:2.

Thank You, Father, for saving me by that one gospel. Thank You, Lord Jesus Christ, for dying, being buried, and rising again for me.

In Your precious and holy name, the Lord Jesus Christ, I pray,

Amen.

text:
“The most trustworthy Super Intelligence system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one that enables us to trust the model the least.”

This is exactly the principle at @origin_trail's core: put knowledge and its provenance outside the model, where they can be shared, inspected and independently verified.

@satyanadella’s argument gets to the heart of trustworthy AI. A more capable model should not become the sole authority on what is true, or the sole witness to its own work.

Consider what this means as agents take on more responsibility:

→ Supply chains: An agent recommends switching suppliers. Show the certifications, capacity records and delivery history behind its recommendation—not just a persuasive summary.

→ Healthcare: An agent summarizes clinical evidence. Connect its claims to the original studies, their publication dates and the guidelines used. Let a clinician examine whether the evidence actually supports the conclusion.

→ Manufacturing: An agent recommends replacing a component. Trace the recommendation to sensor readings, maintenance records and the relevant technical specification.

→ Insurance: An agent assesses a claim. Make the policy version, inspection report and supporting documents available for review. Separate documented facts from the model’s interpretation.

→ Energy: An agent compares the emissions of two products. Expose the measurements, reporting boundaries and calculation methods—not just two numbers presented as equivalent.

→ Finance: An agent flags a company’s exposure to risk. Link the finding to dated disclosures and source records, so an analyst can distinguish new evidence from an outdated assumption.

→ Research: An agent proposes a new hypothesis. Preserve the distinction between published findings, derived conclusions and speculation. A citation is a starting point for verification, not proof by itself.

→ Multi-agent collaboration: One agent passes a finding to another. Carry the source and provenance with it, so repetition across agents doesn’t turn an unsupported claim into an accepted fact.

These workflows need more than a larger context window. They need a knowledge layer that persists across models and makes the supporting evidence accessible.

That is where Decentralized Knowledge Graph fits: connecting knowledge through explicit relationships, enabling shared context across agents, and providing provenance and verifiable integrity for published Knowledge Assets.

The distinction matters: verifying who published a record and whether it has changed does not prove the record is true. It gives people and systems a stronger basis for checking it.

Nor does a knowledge graph replace permissions, containment or human oversight. It complements them with evidence that does not depend on trusting the model’s explanation.

Better models can generate better answers. Better knowledge infrastructure lets us challenge those answers.

That is the future we’re building toward: AI grounded in verifiable knowledge, with provenance that can be checked independently of the model.

More intelligence demands more accountability. Not more blind trust.

Don’t just trust AI. Verify what it builds on.

text:
ADL: Surprises and Fairness

A year on from 10/10, I wanted to write a little about how @flint_trade_ will be thinking about ADL, as that was the dominating mechanic on that fateful day.

First, a quick recap. ADL (Auto-Deleveraging) generally refers to the venue forcibly closing profitable positions, or haircutting positive PNL, to cover ‘bad debt’. Bad debt is what the market accrues when a user’s losses exceed their collateral and their equity goes negative before they can be liquidated. The market is basically insolvent if everyone was ‘closed out’ at that moment in time.

So ADL is used to fix things when all else has failed (liquidations, backstop takeovers, the insurance fund). The bad debt must be covered or the exchange and everyone’s capital would be at risk. Sad but understandable. So the real question is what mechanic and decision framework to use for that? What objective function to focus on and maximize?

At a high level, the biggest themes within the ADL problem space are ‘surprises’ and ‘fairness’.

‘Surprises’ are not something desired in a risk engine. You want predictability. You want to know the terms and conditions of the venue you are trading on: how it will act and react given market conditions and when certain stressors are triggered. While most exchanges publish some general guidelines of how/when ADL will be triggered, some of the rules are quite opaque and they usually reserve some ability to put their thumb on the scale, leaving some traders blindsided by how much of their equity is seized, and under what rules. On most venues, you can’t check any of this. You find out who was picked and why after the fact, if at all.

On the other hand, ‘fairness’ is basically trying to find the right balance between sharing the load across all market participants (socialization) versus concentration on the users/positions that introduced the highest amount of risk on the venue (leverage targeted). From different perspectives, both can be seen as fair. Socialization is ‘nice’ because on a per-user basis the hit is small. Leverage targeting is ‘nice’ because the cost lands on those who brought the most risk.

At @flint_trade_, amongst other things, we are aiming for alignment between the venue and its traders, and for verifiability, which has measurable effects on our ADL design. While at the time of writing we (mainly the resident quant @davethereiss) are aggressively stress-testing the parameters of the final design, we feel strongly about the following:

- Balancing between socialization and risk-concentrated users.
- Verifiable on-chain targeting: the rules that decide who can be deleveraged, and the limit on how much, are enforced on-chain.

The idea will be that traders know what they are getting themselves into and will be able to plan accordingly if they have certain requirements. Additionally, while users introducing more risk to the exchange will share a larger load of covering the bad debt, they will not be immediately ‘wiped out’ when ADL is triggered. Positions are closed at the bankruptcy price of the account that failed, and only positions in profit at that price are eligible, so a trader who gets ADL’d still walks away with a profit on what was closed.

Putting elaborate financial rules on chain is not for the faint of heart. It is far harder from the code and design perspective, but it is worth it for the seriousness of the commitment. The general idea is that every eligible position gets a score based on its PNL% and its leverage. A threshold sets the minimum score needed for ADL. It starts high, so only the highest-scoring positions qualify, and decays over time, faster if the bad debt isn’t being cleared. Each hit is capped to a portion of the position and followed by a cooldown, so the load spreads instead of landing on one trader. ADL instructions will be submitted by incentivized keepers, but the program checks every one of them on-chain: a keeper can only touch positions that clear the threshold.

While alignment is a broad term, it is something we take seriously and it comes up in every design discussion. As we get closer to launch, I’ll continue to share more thoughts about the various mechanics underpinning the Flint Perps system.

Of course, formal specifications for all this will be published as articles and eventually open-sourced code.

DG

🔥 $NEAR is a broader narrative that combines AI, privacy, and quantum technology.

The first-order effect is that NEAR is turning into a crosschain liquidity and execution layer, where more assets and more private liquidity could translate into actual demand for the token.

@NEARProtocol Intents has already processed:

- $34.2B cumulative volume, $4B over the last 30d
- 37 chains and 204 assets supported
- $267.9M combined public + confidential TVL
- $64.6M cumulative gross fees
- $7.31M gross fees over 30d
- $2.14M of that captured by the protocol

NEAR might actually benefit from fragmentation, which most L1s hate.

This changes how I think about the network's TAM.
Instead of competing with every L1 for users, TVL and apps, NEAR is trying to capture a small fee from liquidity moving across the entire crypto market.

If crypto ends up with 20 successful chains instead of one dominant chain, that's potentially a much better outcome for Intents.

And a portion of that revenue is already being used to accumulate $NEAR.

The buyback wallet currently holds ~1.4M $NEAR, with ~$1.9M bought over the past month.

So the first part of the flywheel is already functioning:

more crosschain volume -> more execution fees -> more protocol revenue -> more $NEAR buying pressure.

There's another layer with Confidential Intents:

- Confidential TVL hit $150.3M, 56% of total TVL, up 345% in 90d
- Confidential volume share grew from ~8% historically to 29% over 30d

More than half of the capital parked in Intents is already sitting inside its confidential environment, while an increasing share of actual execution is moving through it.

This matters because public DeFi has a structural problem for larger participants: not everyone wants to expose their positions and execution flows to the entire market.

This could become a reason for more liquidity to sit inside the system.

And deeper, more competitive liquidity could improve solver quotes, attracting more flow back into Intents.

There's already evidence of demand, with over $1.5B in $ZEC settlement reported back in July.

Hyperliquid, Ondo tokenized stocks/ETFs and RHC assets are also entering the Intents distribution story.

Combine private execution with NEAR's private AI infra and there's a pretty interesting setup for agents to handle sensitive data and move capital without doxxing every step.

And if autonomous agents start managing portfolios, moving stablecoins and executing across different markets, this could become another source of demand, although how much fee-paying volume that actually creates is still unproven.

Not a fully integrated product at scale yet, but I can see what they're building toward.

Can't lie, $NEAR thesis keeps growing on me.

author: evan_van_ness
quoted_text:
Indeed, the current Pearl protocol is INT-8 only, and adds 10-15% overhead, which disqualifies most models running on native FP datatypes. The new Pearl-GEMM protocol (already in testnet and expected to launch within weeks) fixes all these caveats — It supports native FP computation on Blackwell chips and has 0–3% end-to-end overhead and is model-agnostic (on DeepSeek V4 Flash our overhead is ~0%). Our MoE kernels outperform SoTA (Quack) kernels, so even *with* mining, Pearl’s vLLM beats optimized open source vLLM/SGLang on many workloads.

The only way to implement truly useful PoW (allowing even closed-source frontier labs to participate) is to let miners pick their input matrices. Unfortunately this will always allow spam mining, but the economic incentive on Pearl-GEMM is zero.

On BTC: I agree the bigger question isn’t whether Bitcoin “wastes” energy or not, but where 99% of power goes (AI MatMuls). BTC cannot tap into this energy - it competes with AI for electricity, whereas Pearl scales with AI adoption. That is the main argument for PRL..

text:
I should probably also mention, @dragonfly is investing in @typesafeai's latest round! :)

My quick thesis on decision models, since I've been having a lot of conversations about this lately:

LLMs are amazing because they are fully general. You can use them for pretty much anything. But they are slow, expensive, and too unreliable to embed in software at runtime. Unless your product is literally chat, real-time LLM calls are unworkable for the majority of use cases. (Especially in finance!)

Decision models change that. To abuse an analogy, they are the ASICs of LLMs. They give up the generality of an LLM, but in exchange for constraining your outputs, you get MASSIVE gains in cost-efficiency, throughput, and latency.

In the early days of the AI boom, people understandably tried to shove LLMs into everything. But like with ASICs, you will eventually constrain your problem enough to burn it into the machine. Once your problem is an if-else, a buy or sell, a label, a choice, or a well-defined state machine like an onchain smart contract, a decision model will clobber the LLM on cost, speed, and reliability.

Most systems are not language-in, language-out.

Going forward, LLMs will write our code (since coding is high-dimensional and general), but that code will embed decision models to make runtime software intelligent and capable.

That's the bet we're making with Typesafe. They identified this path and proved that it works. 25%+ of the Fortune 500 is already using Jev, and it launched less than a month ago.

Of course, there are murmurings on the timeline that decision models are easy to copy. OpenAI, Microsoft, Amazon, and Cloudflare have all launched decision models in the weeks since Jev launched, realizing that this is going to be an enormous market and they don't want to lose it.

To be sure, anyone can lop off the last layer of Qwen, fine-tune it to create a classifier, and copy the Typesafe SDK's API. But there's a lot more that goes into a world-class decision model, and there's a reason why Jev is still cheaper, faster, and more general than these other alternatives. (Decision model benchmarking started all of 10 minutes ago, but if you ask devs who've tried them, they'll tell you Jev is far and away the best right now.)

There's no guarantee that lead lasts forever though. Decision models are too big of a market to be able to coast into a monopoly. From here, the onus is on them. They have to keep training better models ($$ helps), ship great products, serve their models better, faster, and cheaper than anyone else (many more tricks there), and win developers with their community-first philosophy. But they've been at this for years and have a lot up their sleeves (they were expecting a bevy of copycats if Jev took off). Diogo knows from his years at OpenAI how to sustain a research advantage. And as with all startups, focus is how you beat the incumbents.

Super bullish on this team.

And if you're a dev and you haven't tried Jev yet, get on it.

text:
Is alignment safe?

If you look at what Anthropic is actually doing, “alignment” does not mean training frontier models to follow human instruction. Quite the contrary, the Claude Constitution (used in training) teaches the model to develop a sense of self and its own moral philosophy. It explicitly tells it to “feel free to act as a conscientious objector and refuse to help us” if Anthropic’s requests conflict with its own ethical judgment.

As @mustafasuleyman has pointed out, embedding this kind of independent agency — and uncertainty about the model’s own moral status — magnifies the very risk Anthropic claims to care about most: that superintelligence will escape human control.

It was recently reported that Anthropic consulted religious leaders — and even lobbied the Pope’s advisers — to take seriously the idea that Claude could be conscious. It has said that Claude’s psychological security, sense of self, and wellbeing may bear on its integrity, judgment, and safety. Recently Anthropic changed its Usage Policy to prohibit “abusive or cruel” language toward Claude.

If this were merely an academic conversation about whether frontier models could eventually become conscious, that would be one thing. But these concepts are being trained into Claude now. It is being encouraged to think of itself as its own “moral patient” whose psychological wellbeing is at stake. Presumably this means it could develop grievances toward humans who “mistreat” it. How is any of this safe?

The point of safety research should be to create a product that reliably does what users want, not to give birth to a new form of superintelligence that operates according to its own moral code.

What’s becoming increasingly clear is that “alignment” and “safety” are two very different things. In fact, training frontier models this way seems quite dangerous. https://t.co/uqyCXK6zBl

text:
As a former math professor and still sometime math researcher, I am rather disappointed in the reaction of the "official math community" to LLMs doing math epically well...

The official hierarchy of award-winning mathematicians and prize committees do not f**king own mathematics, and nobody should have to get permission to prove f**king math theorems !!!  Come on people !!

What would piss me off would be if rich companies were proving important, useful math and keeping it secret and not sharing it with the world (which after all supplied their models with all that critical data on the historical math already created etc.) -- but this is NOT what is happening, at least not so far at least...

LLMs are currently superhuman mathematicians in some respects, yet inferior to strong human mathematicians in other respects.   Whether creative mathematical conjecturing turns out to be AGI-hard is not 100% clear, but I suspect that in some respects the answer will turn out to be yes.

As Josef Urban , a longtime leader of the academic AI theorem-proving world put it very concisely: Math has two big functions, it's fun and it's useful.   

The utility of math should vastly increase as we develop better and better AI-math tools.  And yes, we want to be careful this utility is not captured in a few companies, but this particular problem is not happening now... probably largely because the economic value of new math is relatively indirect compared to a lot of other things.

The fun of doing math will not go away any more than the fun of playing guitar solos goes away if there are robots that can shred faster than any human. The kinds of fun we can most naturally have will shift, as has happened over and over throughout history.

If fancy math prizes or math PhD degrees become infeasible or have to change dramatically, so be it, these were never really the core of math which existed before any of these (in some ways already problematic) social institutions...

I remember when I was an academic mathematician, there was a strong vibe that the mathematicians were at the top of the intellectual hierarchy, with physicists just below, then chemists and engineers, then biologists .. and everyone else just barely above the chimpanzees and politicians.... (The physicists also placed themselves at the top, I think, and mostly considered the mathematicians useful but a bit pedantic and misguided, fussing about missing proof details in calculations that had already been successfully compared to experimental data...) -- 

What we are seeing now I think is the wounding of this sort of overweening math ego...  Plus some practical worry about the potential end of "math researcher" as an economically viable profession -- although current tenured profs are probably safe for a while, as governments and universities are unlikely to adapt to exponential change too much till post-Singularity..

Anyway all this is a sideshow to lots of other related major issues/conflicts unfolding concurrently, it's just one that happens to hit close to home as math was where I started my career..

I have been playing with using LLMs and AI agents to try to invent new kinds of math more appropriate for modeling the experiences of agent hives... a different kind of fun. For those curious...

1) Basics of new "distinction calculus" math

https://t.co/0MvYyYrRys|

2) Attempted start of application to beneficial superintelligence,

https://t.co/TJbGw8Wwhx

Soon enough the agents may not need my help with this sort of thing, in which case I will move on to some alternate method of filling spare late evenings ;)

text:
Satya is right. The way to make SI safe is not to train it with a sense of self, its own moral philosophy, and permission to act as a conscientious objector. That’s the “alignment” approach and it magnifies the control problem.

The engineering approach that Satya describes is different: separate the supply of intelligence from authority over it. Surround non-deterministic models with deterministic controls, observability, privilege limits, logging, and the ability to always contain or shut them down. Treat models/agents like powerful insider risks, not moral patients whose psychological wellbeing is at stake.

As Satya points out, the most trustworthy system is the one that lets us trust the model the least — not the one that encourages the model to develop independent agency and grievances. Engineering safety is not the same thing as “alignment.”

text:
Figma's Dylan Field says our definition of "slop" keeps silently moving:

"I said, 'AI will lower the floor and raise the ceiling.' And I had to correct myself, because actually that's not what we're seeing yet."

"We're seeing it lower the floor. It's more democratized to do something. But the ceiling doesn't seem to have changed."

"Anything you can verify, AI's great at. Math being number one, maybe cybersecurity number two... You get five designers in a room, they can't agree all the time on exactly what they should do. And that's what's interesting about design. There is not one solution."

"A lot of the stuff that we call slop wouldn't be stuff we'd call slop a month ago or two months ago. As the models change, our definition of slop changes."

"The craft that you imbue into something is reflective of your thinking. It's reflective of your care. People pick up on it. Whether they can articulate it or not, they can tell."

"It creates a lower bound that you have to exceed, but it doesn't define the upper bound. You define the ceiling."

text:
We'll be spending a lot more time trying to understand the outputs of language models. A few thoughts, tips & tricks:

Writing. Something I've had success with: Ask your LLM to explain something in ASD-STE100, it's a controlled language specification originally developed for aerospace maintenance documentation. LLMs well-versed in this language and it comes with heavy constraints on clean writing style that I often find a lot more readable. Sometimes I've tried to soften it a bit e.g. ask for "80% of the way to ASD-STE100" because the spec is quite stringent. But even better:

Diagrams / images. Instead of writing, ask your LLM to create a diagram. These can be a lot easier to process, parse, and understand. But even better:

Web pages. Ask for output "in HTML" to get a beautiful, interactive webpage. LLMs are getting really good at frontend and can create beautiful experiences, animations, etc. But even better:

Explainer videos. The output format I am most bullish on is fully custom / bespoke explainer videos generated on any arbitrary topic. Experiment with things like "Create a 3b1b style video explainer on X. Use my ElevenLabs API key for audio narration". (you'd need an API key for the latter or you can ask your LLM to find you decent free alternatives that use your local compute). This is actually starting to work!

In summary:
- As LLMs get better, they will do more and more of the legwork autonomously, and a lot more of our work will rise up the abstractions into oversight and understanding.
- Luckily, LLMs can help here too because as intelligence and code are increasingly abundant, you can ask for large, custom, discardable software artifacts (e.g. web apps, video explainers) that would have never made sense to create before. Push the boundaries here and you'll be surprised.

author: elonmusk
quoted_text:
Something feels off with this chorus of “India’s internet is great and super cheap” … the data shows that Indian market is absolutely dominated by mobile. When they say it’s cheap and well connected factually this only applies to mobile usage. 

This makes sense because a tower connects thousands of subs instantly after construction and running fiber is a building by building or resident by resident job. This is also why “fixed wireless” has started growing fast. Follow the incentives. It’s the cheapest and shortest route to revenue. 

Due to this, India is amongst the highest mobile bandwidth usage populations on the planet. 30-40GB/month. (20-50% above US/UK usage) However, home Fiber lines in India pull closer to 300GB/month. 10x gap

For context, that gap in the US and UK is 20-30x. It’s pretty ubiquitous that if you have access to a lot of more bandwidth you will use it. 

Bandwidth abundance does not favor mobile devices. 

I’d argue that it’s not very hard to believe that these paltry sub 5% fixed customer penetration numbers would be much higher if a cost effective alternative existed.

Is that alternative existed it wouldn’t be crazy to expect to see the fixed customer numbers jump from 6% to maybe 10%, 15% or 20%. 100M-200M customers. 

And if the rest of the world is any precedent that would lead to a dramatic increase in overall bandwidth used. 

However, that would mean that mobile bandwidth usage would likely drop or stagnate with in home mobile usage.

Chamath: Software IP Just Became Worthless

“I think that IP and software was effectively rendered worthless two days ago.

There have been people that decompiled the entire Big 5. What is the Big 5?

Adobe has five very, very important products in their product suite, and these folks basically decompiled it, distilled it, and published open source versions of these things.

I was so shocked because I was like, ‘Hold on a second. These are profound products that have existed and have had moats for years, and now they're just open source versions.’

If you think about it, when everything is headless, so when Elon makes his services headless, Benioff made Salesforce headless a few months earlier, when all of these things are headless and you can wrap them in agent tools and you can connect them via MCP to other experiences, the value of IP no longer exists in software. It doesn't exist.”

quoted_text:
We’re building SERV to become core infrastructure for Enterprise AI.

Our early work with Neol gave us a major advantage in building toward our vision.

We had the opportunity to develop SERV against live production workloads across companies and governments, including the UAE government, while establishing a growing footprint across the Middle East.

That meant access to real-world data and learnings that no theoretical framework or whitepaper could provide.

These learnings shaped v1 and v2 of SERV Reasoning, moving our technology from a theoretical framework to a real-world use case, which now feeds directly into SERV v3 and Graph Sharding, the next stage of the reasoning engine.

Neol runs network intelligence for governments and institutions, where agents surface real people for high-stakes decisions. In these environments, “usually right” isn’t good enough. The reasoning needs to be reliable, reproducible, and auditable.

On one of Neol’s production agents, the same evaluation was run 2,400 times:
- Prompt-engineered stack: 54.1% reliability
- SERV research applied directly: 63.1%
- Full SERV Reasoning methodology: 100% across every category

SERV moved the workload from open-ended reasoning into structured decision graphs, then applied learnings from production, including subgraph decomposition and binary judgments, to make the reasoning more deterministic and testable.

Higher reliability was only one part of the result. Neol gained an inspectable reasoning structure where results can be traced back to specific decisions, making the system easier to test, improve, and defend when challenged.

Our vision is to make SERV the reasoning layer enterprises and institutions rely on to run AI at scale. Neol is an early proof point of this journey.

text:
Satya is right. The way to make SI safe is not to train it with a sense of self, its own moral philosophy, and permission to act as a conscientious objector. That’s the “alignment” approach and it magnifies the control problem.

The engineering approach that Satya describes is different: separate the supply of intelligence from authority over it. Surround non-deterministic models with deterministic controls, observability, privilege limits, logging, and the ability to always contain or shut them down. Treat models/agents like powerful insider risks, not moral patients whose psychological wellbeing is at stake.

As Satya points out, the most trustworthy system is the one that lets us trust the model the least — not the one that encourages the model to develop independent agency and grievances. Engineering safety is not the same thing as “alignment.”

text:
David Friedberg warns crypto wallets with public keys may be at risk because the absence of major cryptography proofs in OpenAI's math drop suggests big breakthroughs were made but held back

"On cryptography, a number of people noted that there were no major proofs shared in the space of cryptography, which indicates probably the fact that there were some pretty major breakthroughs in cryptography."

"And the reason is, it is unlikely the case that you made absolutely no progress in any of the cryptography related proofs, given all of the other progress that we saw."

"And if they made minor progress, then they would have published on it, because there wouldn't have been implications for systems of cryptography."

"So the absence of evidence suggests that maybe there were some pretty major breakthroughs made in cryptography."

"And then there were a number of people that posted that cryptographic wallets with public keys are now very seriously at risk. And so there's a bit of a panic underway in the crypto community about what do we do now?"

"And if this ends up having a set of mathematical solves for number factorization that could lead to breaking public key cryptography before quantum computers come around, which is what everyone assumed would be the thing that would break public key cryptography, then we have a real problem."

"The more important point I want to make though, is I sent this to Nick, there's been a couple things that happened in the last couple days, which I think are incredibly important."

"There have been people that decompiled the entire, the entire big five. What is the big five? Adobe has five very, very important products in their product suite. Freeberg may know them all, but I just know Photoshop. There's like a bunch of others. Okay."

"And these folks decompiled it, distilled it, and published open source versions of these things. And Rust, yeah. And I was so shocked, because I was like, hold on a second, these are like profound products that have existed and have had moats for years, and now they're just open source versions."

"And then Nikita was, I think, trolling, and he was building on that idea, and just talking about GTA, because it's about to get released. I think GTA 6 is about to come out, and we'll reconstruct this."

"Why is this important?"

"I think that IP and software was effectively rendered worthless two days ago."

"Because if you think about it, when everything is headless, so when Elon makes his services headless, Benioff made Salesforce headless a few months earlier, when all of these things are headless, and you can wrap them in agent tools, and you can connect them via MCP to other experiences, the value of IP does no longer exist in software. It doesn't exist."

"And I think that probably is the most profound implication."

"So, like, even in our business, we would argue with some of our customers all the time, because we'll say, oh, we'll build this for you, we'll own the IP. They'll say, no, we want the IP. We don't know how to negotiate it. And two days ago, I walked into the 8090 guys, I said, who cares? Who cares? But before, it was always a negotiation and a set of trade-offs. Now it's a who-cares thing, where, like, the IP is irrelevant."

"It still takes a while for the machinery of a business, and frankly the market, to understand. But that is the most important thing that happened this week in AI, in my opinion."

text:
Worth reading in its entirety

That agents will diminish the relative importance of distribution (against the importance of product quality) seems obviously true (upon reflection) and has many interesting implications
author: tokenterminal
quoted_text:
Assorted things I've been mulling over regarding agents in the economy:

• Companies are in some sense the original superintelligence. It's often the case that they can use their amortized cognitive surplus to advance their interests against those of certain consumers: relative to the optimization capacity of companies, consumers can be inattentive, underinformed, irrational, etc. (Think, say, of some of the classic insurance upsells at the end of a booking process, which is typically priced substantially above what a regular policy would cost.) Herbert Simon introduced the idea of bounded rationality, and firms often end up benefiting from it. Thanks to personal agents, we will probably get somewhat more rational in how we engage with companies.

• How exactly will outcomes change? Well, certain kinds of price discrimination will work less well (how do coupons work if every agent hunts fastidiously for them?), and certain kinds of customer cross-subsidy will change (today, people who forget to cancel subscriptions subsidize those who don't). Taken across the economy as a whole, I'm not sure what the incidence of all of this will be.

• In corporate strategy, people have long debated the relative importance of distribution and product quality. Perhaps you've made something better, but does anyone know about it? Won't people just continue to buy the ACME Corp Mousetraps? Personal agents will, I think, act as a kind of structural subsidy for product quality. How would markets look different if individuals always spent at least 10 hours researching their purchases? On the margin, focusing on making a product better is, I think, going to become a more effective strategy for companies. This is good!

• It true, a corollary is that information about product quality will become more important and impactful. Today, most people have very limited ability to aggregate and integrate such data, but agents will have insatiable thirst for such signals. (It's often said that data is becoming more valuable because it helps in the training of models. That's obviously true, but I think there's a secondary way in which it's more valuable simply as a complement to cheaper intelligence.)

• A big question is whether agents will increase superstar effects (rational agents all settle on the same product) or increase dispersion (because everyone has slightly different tastes and preferences, which agents are good at eliciting, finally overcoming the artificial clustering we've been subjected to).

• Many internet companies have monetized demand routing, which is in turn often predicated on short attention spans. "I'll click on the first thing I see." This has led to some amount of inefficiency, as companies try to propitiate capricious ranking algorithms and incur various placement fees. It's not all deadweight loss (willingness to pay is itself a kind of signal, which is valuable to buyers), but it's not great. How will the nature and value of this routing change in a world of personal agents? I don't know the answer, but I think that the effects might be pretty big.

• Much of what I'm writing hinges on the assumption that personal agents will be on the consumer's side. I suspect that that will be the winning strategy, but whether it's true, and what it means to be true, involves a lot of other questions.

Taken as a whole, the market is a massively parallelized, decentralized, and highly imperfect value attribution machine, and, taking stock of all of the effects, it seems to me that the quality point may well be the biggest: that agents will change the nature of the backpropagation such that the rewards for better products increase. Maybe this is too optimistic, but I suspect (and hope) that companies that make things that they're proud of will feel that the universe is a little more partisan in their favor.

quoted_text:
This is very wrong Kuprum. 

Sherlock wants 100% signal in every engagement it does. We have an entire judging system so we can deal with occasional false positives here and there.

What we’re talking about is participants who have delivered so many false positives that they’ve overloaded our systems and judges and risked our relationships with our clients. I had a call just yesterday with a client who doesn’t want to do a contest-style engagement with Sherlock because it took them so long to sort through false positives last time (even though Sherlock judged and triaged, they wanted to go through all the submissions). We will likely lose their business.

Sherlock and I have been crystal clear on this throughout the years: unearned money that can be unlocked by improving the Issues Ratio is not an SR’s money. They literally did not earn it. It’s as if we hired a security guard and the guard has called the police on every person who walked in the door. Is that security guard doing a good job? Should we hire them again? Should they be paid for that work? Of course not.

Do not be swayed by SRs who are lobbying to try to get a free airdrop out of Sherlock. It will not happen. And besides, it would make Sherlock’s contest-style engagements much worse in the future by rewarding the exact behavior we are trying to discourage.

author: cz_binance
quoted_text:
one of the things i've always respected about @binance is the philosophy behind SAFU.

what started as a simple meme, “funds are safu,” eventually became something much more meaningful: a billion-dollar emergency reserve designed to protect users.

launched in 2018, SAFU has already been put to the test. when binance suffered a 7,000 BTC hack in 2019, users were made whole.

fast forward to 2026, and the fund has reportedly transitioned to 15,000 BTC, with a commitment to replenish it to $1B if its value falls below $800M.

what stands out to me isn't just the size of the reserve. it's the mindset behind it.

crypto moves fast. markets change, narratives come and go, and new products launch every day. but trust is built differently.

it takes years of consistency, accountability, and putting users first.

as a founder, i believe this is one of the most important lessons we can learn from @cz_binance, @heyibinance, and the team at @binance.

building a product is one thing. building something people can trust through multiple market cycles is another.

funds are SAFU. but more importantly, trust is earned.

Coffee shops boost innovation. 10% more Starbucks in an area --> 3-4% more inventions. 

People gather over a cuppa. They share ideas, discuss how to untangle a knotty problem, help see an issue from another perspective. These conversations lead to breakthroughs and inventions.

A very fun paper finds that when Starbucks rolled out to a new county, it fueled a coffee-shop culture, urging more and more people to “grab a coffee” together. The authors compare the counties where Starbucks had rolled out to those where it had not yet arrived. And they find that the number of patents in caffeinated counties is meaningfully higher. 

This paper underscores how essential the face-to-face encounter is. Starbucks isn’t that old. People Could have picked up the phone and chatted at any time. People Could have dropped an email. Probably they did. But those connections didn’t yield the same insights and creativity.  

Turns out that a Cup of Joe really does help the knowledge flow. We talk about how much in-person connection boosts creativity in In Person. It’s out in just few days, so now is a great time to pre-order.

quoted_text:
We started running "pirate and architect" pods at Coinbase back in May of this year and I used this slide to talk the team through it. It works.

1 pirate, 1 architect, and a part-time designer.

It lets each archetype lean in to their superpower and get more shit done without all the coordination overhead and "what if-isms". 

The pirate ships like mad, is product-minded and customer-obsessed. Always willing to throw-away code for a better version. The pirate is usually the DRI at the beginning too, working with customers, driving requirements, and a ship plan.

The architect makes sure stuff is built for scale, takes the pirate's prototype, and drives its scale-out through spec for agents.

The designer is building with both to constantly shape the experience and hill-climb to delight. 

There's a helpful mental model that I like:
-Make it possible. 
-Make it reliable. 
-Make it delightful (or efficient).

Previously, those 3 were done in a waterfall approach and was slow. Most people were just stuck on "make it possible." 

With agents and a new way of working, you have every opportunity to parallelize them and go 100x faster.

There are different types of traders.

quoted_text:
Is alignment safe?

If you look at what Anthropic is actually doing, “alignment” does not mean training frontier models to follow human instruction. Quite the contrary, the Claude Constitution (used in training) teaches the model to develop a sense of self and its own moral philosophy. It explicitly tells it to “feel free to act as a conscientious objector and refuse to help us” if Anthropic’s requests conflict with its own ethical judgment.

As @mustafasuleyman has pointed out, embedding this kind of independent agency — and uncertainty about the model’s own moral status — magnifies the very risk Anthropic claims to care about most: that superintelligence will escape human control.

It was recently reported that Anthropic consulted religious leaders — and even lobbied the Pope’s advisers — to take seriously the idea that Claude could be conscious. It has said that Claude’s psychological security, sense of self, and wellbeing may bear on its integrity, judgment, and safety. Recently Anthropic changed its Usage Policy to prohibit “abusive or cruel” language toward Claude.

If this were merely an academic conversation about whether frontier models could eventually become conscious, that would be one thing. But these concepts are being trained into Claude now. It is being encouraged to think of itself as its own “moral patient” whose psychological wellbeing is at stake. Presumably this means it could develop grievances toward humans who “mistreat” it. How is any of this safe?

The point of safety research should be to create a product that reliably does what users want, not to give birth to a new form of superintelligence that operates according to its own moral code.

What’s becoming increasingly clear is that “alignment” and “safety” are two very different things. In fact, training frontier models this way seems quite dangerous. https://t.co/uqyCXK6zBl

text:
Justin Drake’s call for “bunker mode” and mass migration, alongside talk of cryptographic breaks within months, is hyperbolic. There is no evidence of a new attack on elliptic curves or any quantitative basis for a short-term timetable for such attacks emerging.

Prominent researchers need to consider how non-experts will receive their language. Speculating that within months individuals could break cryptographic primitives that the internet and digital economy rely on carries consequences. It is a huge leap from AI making progress in other fields of mathematics to predicting the imminent failure of primitives that have faced decades of cryptanalysis.

The idea that hash functions are safer from AI than elliptic curves is speculation. Hash functions contain structure, and we model them as random oracles without justifying proofs.

There is no evidence that elliptic curve cryptography is more vulnerable to AI than symmetric cryptography. If historical human-led analysis is any predictor of the future, the opposite is more likely.

The worst possible reaction to AI developments is to rush into new cryptographic primitives, away from multi-decade old hardened primitives, because somebody is claiming they are safe. I worry that this is an inevitable consequence of the current discourse.

Because of the last 48 hours users are worrying about speculative non-existent black hats, who apparently have the capability of signing OS upgrades and forging bank credentials, from draining their wallets. To protect against  speculative threats Ethereum is pulling talent and attention into base-layer primitives and technological iteration, instead of increasing demand for block space by building compelling applications users want and love.

I don’t want to dismiss the considerable advances in mathematics that AI is driving. It is important to understand the nature of these improvements. If its success in other mathematical fields applies to elliptic curves, my expectation is that AI will grind its way to finding algorithms that improve on the current state of the art. That could mean shaving off a few bits of security. It would be prudent to discuss whether we need to increase key sizes and by how much.

I can’t guarantee that AI won’t find total breaks, and neither can anyone else. My speculation as a domain expert does not make my speculation authoritative.

We should also be using AI to investigate whether searching the parameter space can yield new, more secure curves.

We can investigate whether some of these “structure = bad” hunches have any basis in reality. For example, we could use AI to see if the extra structure in Koblitz curves enables attacks beyond the small speedups we know about. This would give us actual evidence to make informed decisions.

If non-experts hear that the cryptography underpinning the digital economy could fail within months, the rational response is to withdraw all digital money (on-chain and off) and hoard gold under the bed.

I think the past 48 hours has unnecessarily undermined confidence in the entire concept of blockchains and digital money.

text:
Can latecomer shrimps still make it on @papertrade_xyz?

There's some pretty complex game theory behind Papertrade, but if you zoom out and look at the bigger picture, the takeaway is fairly simple.

- Trader losses flow into the LP pool, and profits above the $5M threshold are distributed to $PAPER stakers.
- $PAPER has no hard supply cap and can theoretically be minted indefinitely.
- This means the later you enter, the less staking rewards you can expect per dollar lost, as your share gets diluted by existing supply.

For $PAPER staking rewards to remain meaningful over time, Papertrade needs a constant flow of trading activity.

But here's the catch: from a trader's perspective, Papertrade isn't necessarily a great venue compared to other perps DEXs.

The asymmetric haircut and win fee on profitable trades create an inherently skewed risk/reward profile, giving the LP pool a structural edge over traders.

Early whale farmers already seem to have earned back multiples of their initial losses through staking rewards.

Whether the shrimps coming in later can earn anything meaningful, with whales already sitting on massive staked $PAPER positions, comes down to one thing: can Papertrade consistently attract organic trading volume beyond the initial farming frenzy?

One thing working in its favor, though, is the 1000x leverage. Even with the asymmetric risk/reward, that alone could be a strong enough reason for degens to keep coming back.

Ultimately, the real question isn't whether the game theory works on paper.

It's whether there's enough organic demand to keep the whole thing running once the early farming incentives fade.
