text:
Brothers Karamazov was Einstein’s favorite novel, a verdict he shared with Freud, Hillary Clinton, and Murakami. Dostoyevsky was Pope Francis’s favorite author. Indeed, he approvingly quoted Elder Zosima; perhaps an interesting case of art molding life. At the risk of betraying my relative shallowness and inferiority, I confess that I did not love it.

Written in the shadow of the death of Dostoyevsky’s son (also Alyosha), and, more broadly, after a life of repeated tragedy, Karamazov attempts most of all to address the problem of evil in Christianity. Ivan presents a trenchant argument, asking how the suffering of children may possibly be explained given the existence of a supposedly benevolent God (Dostoyevsky collected real court cases for Ivan), culminating in Ivan’s famous return of the ticket.

The book gives some sense for how dislocating the nineteenth century must have been. The ascendant authority of science, the spread of materialist philosophy, the doctrine of evolution, the aftermath of the French revolution and its supposedly enlightened empiricism: in Karamazov, we get the feeling that finding some kind of consilience wasn’t just an abstract philosophical challenge, but a source of intense spiritual torment. If inherited tradition is no longer an adequate basis for faith, why would we rationally cleave to an apparently irrational theology? All of this was in the air: it was only two years later that Nietzsche declared God to be dead.

Perhaps demonstrating the utility of the novel as a medium, Dostoyevsky does not even attempt to solve the problem, but merely to illustrate a response, showing how individuals (Alyosha, Elder Zosima) may in the face of the inherent injustice present in the world nonetheless pursue lives of benevolence and charity: theodicy-by-example. In so doing, Dostoyevsky tacitly concedes that none of the teetering justifications expounded over the centuries can actually survive critical pressure and be defended through pure logic.

Ultimately, though, I don’t find myself being fully compelled by Dostoyevsky’s characterization of the problem or his proposed solution. As another sprawling confrontation with and attempt to reconcile the problem of evil, Grossman’s Life and Fate is maybe a useful counterpoint. Unlike Karamazov, Life and Fate shows actual people confronting great wickedness. Ikonnikov, a small but important figure, is ordered to help in the construction of a gas chamber. He refuses, with full awareness of the consequences that will ensue. The Karamazovs, by contrast, live middle class lives unvisited by greater events. Ivan has money, education, and leisure; his torment is the invention of his own mind and thus a kind of self-indulgence. Even Alyosha, the novel’s most sympathetic character, is never tested. His crisis is spiritual: there is a slightly comic kerfuffle about Zosima’s noisome corpse, which challenges his faith, but no circumstance requires him to stake his life or even his comfort.

Thus, a fundamental issue with Karamazov is that the problems of the book are on some level fake: they’re the self-inflicted derangements of febrile and dysregulated men. How much can or should we learn from the insane?

To be charitable to Dostoyevsky, we might say that he understood the spiritual dislocation of the era that later gives rise to the larger evils of totalitarianism in the twentieth, even prefiguring them in the Grand Inquisitor. (Dostoyevsky explored this theme in greater detail a few years earlier in Demons.) Camus in 1959: “The real nineteenth century prophet was Dostoevsky, not Karl Marx.” In this interpretation, the problems in Karamazov set the stage for those in Life and Fate.

Maybe. At least as a work of art, I’m not sure that this anticipation is enough to make the book stand on its own. In Karamazov, one continually wonders why the brothers don’t just pull it together. Dostoyevsky seems to transpose his own inner depths and spiritual torment onto his characters, but most people are not tortured writers, and it does not feel that the unhingedness of the characters is ever fully earned.

In attempting to address evil, Grossman’s conclusion is ostensibly similar to Dostoyevsky’s: the only resolution lies in senseless kindness. For Dostoyevsky, this message is embodied in Alyosha, who represents a kind of fervent innocence. For me, however, it’s not clear that Alyosha ever fathoms the realities and extremities of evil, and hence he’s not fully persuasive: does he even reckon with the misdeeds of his brothers?

Grossman is willing to engage head on. Far beyond gruesome newspaper anecdotes or neurotic and volatile siblings, Ikonnikov directly experiences the Holodomor in Ukraine and then the murders of the Jews. He has no patience for the kind of revolutionary ideas that animated Ivan’s contemporaries: “whenever we see [the dawn of an eternal good], the blood of old people and children is always shed.”

Alyosha believes in the Church and is willing to set aside its failures to address suffering. The book closes on his declaration that all shall rise again. That is, Alyosha does not accept the tragedy of Ilyusha, an innocent boy’s death, but rather seeks to deny and escape it. “We shall see each other and shall tell each other with joy and gladness all that has happened.”

Life and Fate flatly rejects providential resolution. The heavens may be empty, and there is no greater meaning in evil. We can simply choose (freedom the other great theme of Life and Fate) to pursue acts of charity, generosity, and comfort:

“Yes, as well as this terrible Good with a capital ‘G’, there is everyday human kindness. The kindness of an old woman carrying a piece of bread to a prisoner, the kindness of a soldier allowing a wounded enemy to drink from his water-flask, the kindness of youth towards age, the kindness of a peasant hiding an old Jew in his loft. The kindness of a prison guard who risks his own liberty to pass on letters written by a prisoner not to his ideological comrades, but to his wife and mother.”

These acts don’t ennoble the suffering but are instead justified on their own terms. Such altruism cannot become a catechism, as clearly lies in Alyosha’s destiny (and Karamazov was planned before Dostoyevsky's death as the first of two works); instead, our kindness must be senseless. And we should presume no salvation in adherence: Alyosha imagines a kind of sacred tutelage, but Ikonnikov is unceremoniously shot.

Karamazov doesn’t show true evil, and Dostoyevsky’s solution, such as it is, involves a kind of denial, or at least evasion through metaphysics. Grossman saw it directly, and instead argues, humanistically, that we should be kind just because.

—

If Dostoyevsky came to his works by trying to understand and depict Russian society, they in turn became tapestries for others to understand national souls.

In the aftermath of WWI, Russia was the great power defined in opposition to the West. As Germany tried to rediscover its own soul in the wreckage of defeat, it looked east to Russia, and frequently to Dostoyevsky himself.

Carl Jung thought that the German people had a kind of Karamazovian quality. In particular, he believed that Christianity had disciplined them without fully transforming the impulses beneath their ostensibly civilized conduct: the “Germanic barbarian” was divided into upper and lower halves. Religion had domesticated the former while leaving the latter untamed. Waning faith consequently threatened to release forces that its authority had long restrained: “As the Christian view of the world loses its authority, the more menacingly will the ‘blond beast’ be heard prowling about in its underground prison, ready at any moment to burst out with devastating consequences. When this happens in the individual it brings about a psychological revolution, but it can also take a social form.”

Dostoyevsky was reputedly invoked on a weekly basis at Max Weber’s Sunday gatherings. At the beginning of Reflections of a Nonpolitical Man, Thomas Mann’s later-repudiated 1918 nationalist polemic, he quotes approvingly Dostoyevsky’s characterization of Germany as the “protesting Western empire”, never quite adopting or feeling at home with the inheritance of Rome. In the same year, Spengler wrote Decline of the West, and explicitly perceived in Russia a youthful vigor, primitiveness, and irrationality that contrasted with the senile high culture of the German and Western worlds. In Magic Mountain, Mann later used Clavdia Chauchat to personify the seductive dangers of Eastern (i.e. Russian) illogic.

Hermann Hesse declared that, for all their differences, Fyodor, Dmitri, Ivan, and Alyosha are actually all of one type; the Russian man. In them, he perceived that “the ideal of the Karamazov, primeval, Asiatic, and occult, is already beginning to consume the European soul”, which was leading to the downfall of Europe. In Hesse’s conception, the Russian man rejects inherited ethics and morals, and even beneficent Alyosha represents an “amoral impartiality.” Man is, Hesse says, halfway between animals and higher consciousness; the former restrained through the process of civilization and domestication. The Karamazovs represent the fraying of the ties.

Hesse proceeds, ominously, to notice that the Germans in particular are more vulnerable than any European people to the temptations of “all those evils which one may regard in different ways, but which collectively signify the Karamazov.” While he was prescient in anticipating some of what would follow, he was in the end too sanguine in his hope that the spiritual dislocation could remain limited to that. “It is possible that the whole Downfall of Europe will play itself out only inwardly, only in the souls of a generation, only in changing the meaning of worn-out symbols, in the dis-valuation of spiritual values.” Alas!

In general, it is interesting to trace the mutual obsession between Russia and Germany: how preoccupied each was with the respective supposedly corrupting influences; how urgent the question of the national soul was felt to be. Many of the analyses seem a bit contradictory—Hesse actually inverts Dostoyevsky, for whom “everything is permitted” nihilism is a Western import for which Russian Orthodoxy is the cure—but there’s a striking intensity in the attempts to apprehend.

Most of all, I’m struck by how anachronistic it all feels today: a country’s writers investigating the national soul and the nation’s fate through the lens of foreign literature.

Which novels or works of art do we use to understand our contemporary issues? Should we be using such works? Do they inform or do they mislead? Today, the US worries a lot about China, but this mostly manifests at the level of trade balances, AI policy, and military prowess. We don’t seem to worry much about the spiritual force of Chinese ideals, and for all of the policy fractiousness, China continues to import and absorb American culture with enthusiasm that is mostly undimmed. There is a genre of jeremiad and cultural analysis in the US that rhymes a little with early twentieth century German criticism, but it today tends to be much more clinical, hinging around PISA scores, smartphones, lower fertility, and not around higher aspirations and ideals as such. So, to what extent should there be analyses of the national soul? And to what extent should they connect with major novels and works of art?

text:
I spent some time talking with and watching @mehul at the @maticrobots booth at @theXtakeover, which was way better this year due to @teslaownersSV getting really banger speakers. @NICKIMINAJ lit up the crowd here.

He makes the cleaning robot that we have in our home and it is a great robot for cleaning the floors.

But I learned long ago to study customers  in booths, since they can tell you a lot about how fast things are being adopted. And how fast consumers are changing.

This was its first attempt at a consumer-oriented booth.

It was packed, but both existing customers and new ones were mixing together and the existing ones were telling them others about how much they loved theirs. I saw several get sold.

Evangelistic behavior by customers grows companies.

But we talked a lot about where robots are today.

He says a humanoid run by all AI is years away. He thinks the problem is bigger than even Tesla can get done quickly and there is so much demand in even his own factories to fulfill before going after homes.

I think Tesla could get there within two years. He says longer. 

But I am like Elon. A timing is often off because I want the future to happen faster and that it often takes a few years longer.

And Mehul knows the robot industry deeper than anyone I know.

Oh and those who buy one robot are easier to convince to buy another. 

Their signage was all about self-driving floor cleaning. Vision only. Totally private. Made in USA. Messages that appeal to Tesla owners.

But I am encouraged. There are buyers for robots, and my past experience shows consumers change quickly once you show a better product than anyone else has.

Oh and he had a part of the booth for children to play and they all loved playing with the robot.

He told me he saw that early too when it was testing out prototypes and spent a lot of time making it safe for kids and babies. And cute, even.

The robot industry should pay attention to Mehul. One of the best consumer products builders I have met. 

2,500 Tesla fans are in Austin this weekend for X Takeover.

text:
Most borrow/lend protocols and ecosystems I spoke to last week want to unlock tokenized stocks on DeFi. 

In one of the recent Yuzu contract upgrades we intentionally included a vault launcher feature for this purpose. Think https://t.co/jBhMkQHEPD memecoin launcher but for vaults. So we can literally launch 100 vaults within a day and build an entire marketplace of vaults for different stocks and strategies -  unlocking one-click deposit carry trade strategies for all sorts of tokenized equities (or assets). 

Tokenized stocks are growing fast but barely used as DeFi collateral (<5% utilization). The problem is unlocking DeFi use on tokenized stocks still requires a multi-step process for users (ie no user friendly UI/UX with one-click feature unlock). The blocker here isn't no use case but rather UI/UX. The feature unlock needs to be one-click. 

Current setups suck and this is what needs to happen. Product layers that turn “borrow against my stocks” into a simple yield strategy (ie Yuzu).

Holders now must still figure out what to do with borrowed stables (Spend IRL? Deploy for yield?). Current flows have too many steps and require users to decide what they want to do, so most capital just sits idle.

Isolated markets also further perpetuates this cold start problem cause lenders have to "guess" the most in-demand tokenized assets to park idle capital now. I'm thinking if an Aave v3 model/Aave Horizon model solves this. A market with pooled capital but isolated to tokenized equities. Have some yield assets in there as well so base USDC/USDT lending rate starts competitive. Similar to how Aave Horizon started with tokenized T-Bills with incentives later JAAA etc. Lenders would then park capital without having to deal with the issue of idle unproductive capifal. first then stock holders have to think of a use case. 

Base lending isn’t enough. The depth of liquidity in tokenized stocks on-chain makes stock lending for shorting imposible. So dont expect a base lending rate anytime soon. Accessing DeFi borrow through tokenized stocks just for pure leverage isn’t the answer as well cause IBKR margin are already competitive (~5.4% on smaller balances, lower on larger ones) with better UX and execution.Perp DEXes win on leverage, speed, and UX. Pure leverage has better alternatives. Carry does not.

The real product is still one-click with these steps all under the hood and only optionally visible to the user. 

Step 1) Deposit tokenized stocks into vault
Step 2) Vault automatically borrows against stock
Step 3) Vault deploy into carry/yield strategies and 
Step 4) Vault manages risk and strategy (LTVs, underlying etc, yield).

Without the UX and the strategy layer, DeFi infrastructure for tokenized equities will stay underused.

Let's talk about $JEANPHIL and $CLAUDIA, and why I'm bullish on the AI Influencer + short-form video narrative.

GTBxUiw6wJdmmkCGZgRHLyYxqu1vG4KtRpeox6yDpump 
2j5SaS7xy776qCBpyPQbZjyQSAtKiFgrwjfErthnW2ZM 

First, the broader sector.

I believe AI Influencers combined with short-form video distribution could become one of the narratives worth watching in the next Meme market cycle.

The underlying logic is simple: AI is turning character creation from a high-cost, low-frequency process into a low-cost, scalable content business that can be operated continuously. In the past, building an influencer required appearance, performance, filming, editing, and long-term management. Now, creators can use AI to design characters, develop personalities, produce short videos, and even operate multiple virtual personas simultaneously.

But what really matters isn't how many characters AI can generate. It's whether those characters can consistently produce content that people want to watch, discuss, and follow.

Short-form video drives distribution, characters accumulate attention, and Memes can become a speculative vehicle for that attention in the crypto market. An AI character can build a distinctive persona through continuous video releases, participate in trending topics, create new memes, and interact with other characters, gradually evolving from a single viral clip into a recognizable IP.

Compared with traditional Memes that rely on an isolated event or a single image, these characters theoretically have the ability to continuously generate new material for distribution. If a character develops a stable audience and cultural recognition, it no longer has to rely entirely on a single viral moment to maintain attention.

If this model gains traction in the crypto market, speculation may shift beyond the next viral image toward AI characters that have already attracted genuine attention on platforms like TikTok and Instagram, can consistently produce content, and have the potential to channel that external attention on-chain.

This is why I've chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA. They represent two different paths within this emerging narrative.

JEANPHIL: External traction that has already emerged.

Jean Phil is an AI-generated French male character. His blond bowl cut, curled mustache, brown houndstooth suit, and signature street-style boxing moves create a recognizable visual identity that is easy to imitate.

The character has attracted significant attention on TikTok and Instagram, generating imitations and derivative content. This demonstrates how an AI character with a distinctive persona and a simple, replicable video format can quickly capture attention on mainstream social platforms.

The logic is straightforward: the character attracts external traffic, the content inspires imitations and remixes, and that attention may eventually flow into its on-chain token.

Compared with Memes that rely solely on narratives originating within crypto, JEANPHIL already has an external source of attention. What it needs to prove next is whether that momentum can persist and whether the character's popularity can translate into sustained token demand.

CLAUDIA: From AI creation toward long-term IP development.

CLAUDIA is more focused on long-term IP development. Around Claudia, anabology has been building Claudia Gallery and proposed creating an open version of Hatsune Miku for the AI era. Related initiatives also include AI character creation tools, Agent Skills, and Claudia Local.

The Influencer mode brings this vision closer to the AI Influencer model: by continuously producing videos, maintaining a consistent character identity, and experimenting with high-frequency publishing, it aims to gradually build its own audience.

The logic is that AI lowers content production costs, continuous video output helps establish character recognition, and the character gradually accumulates an audience before attempting to convert that external attention into IP influence and on-chain interest.

Compared with JEANPHIL, CLAUDIA has greater potential in the direction of a long-term AI creator ecosystem. The goal isn't simply to make a character go viral in the short term, but to explore how an AI character can continuously produce content, build an audience, and develop into an expandable, open IP.

However, this path has a longer chain of validation. Being able to produce videos consistently doesn't mean the content will necessarily gain traction. Having creation tools doesn't guarantee the ability to build a successful character. And an open-IP vision doesn't automatically mean the token can capture the resulting value.

Although both projects fall under the broader AI Influencer narrative, their trading theses are different.

JEANPHIL is more focused on existing external traction. The key question is whether that attention can persist and translate into token demand. CLAUDIA is more focused on AI creation capabilities and long-term IP development. The key question is whether it can consistently produce compelling content and build a genuine audience.

What I'm bullish on is the shared potential behind both approaches: AI characters could evolve beyond static images into dynamic IPs that continuously produce content, participate in trending topics, build social relationships, and generate new Memes.

Of course, a compelling sector narrative doesn't mean every related token will appreciate.

We need to distinguish three separate outcomes: an AI character gaining attention, an IP building lasting influence, and a token capturing value from that influence. A character can become popular without benefiting its token. A project can have impressive creation tools without producing viral content. Even if an IP continues to grow, attention may remain entirely off-chain if the token has no meaningful connection to its development.

Therefore, what I'm really looking for isn't the first token to announce that it uses AI, but projects that have demonstrated their ability to attract external attention, consistently produce distributable content, and establish a clear connection between that attention and their tokens.

AI is the production tool, short-form video is the distribution channel, character IP is the vehicle for attention, and the token represents a separate speculative market.

When these four elements become genuinely connected, AI Influencers could evolve from a trending concept into a new Meme narrative with sustained distribution potential.

That's why I'm bullish on this direction and have chosen to take a deeper look at JEANPHIL and CLAUDIA.

text:
fomo 已经赚了 8000 多万美元，产品确实做得比较扎实

拆开来看，fomo 有效地把链抽象 × 法币入金 × 交易行为社交化等行业里经过 PMF 验证的多个模块，高效地组合到了一起

◦ 链抽象：主打 One account, one balance, any chain. 普通用户无需理解链、跨链、gas 等概念，像 UniversalX 等产品 2024 年已经做得不错了

◦ 法币入金：Moonshot 在 2024 年火了，主打法币入金直接买 meme coin，不过只支持 Solana 链，作为当时的创新产品 7 个月就被 Jupiter 收购了。fomo 延续了这个功能，并支持所有主流公链资产

◦ 交易行为社交化：gmgn 团队 2022 年的上一个产品 NFTTrack，主要功能是关注 KOL 交易 NFT 的动态，把交易行为转化为一种内容。虽然 NFT 整体凉了，但是 NFT 和 meme coin 的共同点都是，交易行为重度受到社区和身边圈子的影响，social driven trading 的内核需求没变

还有一个小功能也挺有意思，用户可以对一笔交易附带 thesis，还能持续更新。即使持仓不变，市场始终有波动和变化，持仓心态的波动也是值得分享的。交流和交易不分家，这些 thesis 可有效地把不同的 traders 连接在一起，形成一个有效的场域。这个功能，雪球的前身「i 美股」也做过，用户添加自选股的时候，可以持续更新对这个公司的 comments.

很多创新不是真的从 0 涌现出来的，而是在对需求深刻理解的基础上，可以站在前人的肩膀上，组合进化而来

text:
🚨 $79AU POOL DRAINED FOR $14.35M DESPITE 79% OF LP RECEIPTS BEING BURNED!

A PancakeSwap pool for $79AU, the token of 79thVault, lost $14.35M in USDT on October 7.

Here’s the scary part: burning LP receipts didn’t protect the liquidity.

🔴 A privileged permission in the token contract allowed authorized wallets to pull tokens from the pool without paying.
🔴 Those tokens were then sold back into the pool for USDT.
🔴 Bitquery identified two wallets with this permission, and simulations suggested around 95% of the remaining $79AU in the pool could still be removed.

The lesson? Burned LP tokens don’t guarantee liquidity is safe if the token contract has dangerous privileges. ⚠️

Always check contract permissions, not just the LP burn percentage.

在今年6-7月期间，我看到过这样一个论断：

2018-2019年熊市，BTC跌了80%+；
2021-2022年熊市，BTC跌了70%+；

所以，2025-2026年熊市，BTC跌幅应该有60%+。按最高12.6w算低点至少要到5w以下。

这里似乎还考虑了本轮ETF和传统资本的介入，跌幅缩小，看上去无比合理，有很多人都会信。

我说的没错吧，大家应该也都有看到过吧？

那么现在，对本轮牛市BTC只能到某某价格（比如最多20w）的预测本质上和上述论断如出一辙。我个人认为这几乎等同于开盲盒。

正如Rounder兄所说，目前我们没有充足的、科学的、客观的理由来预判BTC一定高于或低于某个特定的价格。

即便“说”对了，也只是“巧合”。

----------------------------------------------

最近，我比较喜欢关注一些粉丝数在2k-2w之间的博主。知道为什么吗？

因为在这个阶段是账号运营的关键期，他们会极尽所能的汲取营养，输出高质量内容，来吸引更多的关注，从而推升流量。

他们不能也不会过多的释放噪音。

至少我自己当初在这个阶段，就敢做敢说，敢讲真话，没有顾虑，不绕弯，不回避。

但现在就不同了。

经常一句话，写了又删，删了又写，反复斟酌措辞，避免不必要的误会（尤其是那些躲在暗处等我犯错的黑子们）。

很多时候，明明我内心是“很确定”，但文字却偏偏要写成“有可能”，没办法，这就是理想和现实（订阅区小范围的讲，会好一些）。

所以，我推荐大家去关注这些有内容，有想法，有真实交易经验，且现在账号还处于起步阶段的优秀博主。

Rounder @CryptoRounder 就是其中之一。

我也会找机会帮他们转发引用，把我认可的博主们推荐给各位小伙伴。

如果你也是其中之一，欢迎毛遂自荐。但前提是你要先让我先认识你，了解你，才能推荐你。

text:
Uniswap 将 #Hookr 的 hooks 列入其白名单，对Hookr有何意义：

1、官方路由支持：Uniswap 官方界面的路由算法现在会考虑 Hookr hooks 的池子，用户在主站交易时更容易被路由到这些池子，提升成交量和价格发现效率；

2、更好的流动性和可见度：Hookr 上启动的代币/池子能更自然地接入 Uniswap 主流量，降低“只能在自己前端交易”的摩擦；

3、生态认可：说明 Uniswap Labs 认为该 hook 在路由层面可接受（不恶意、不违规绕过费用等），Hookr 也借此定位为 Uniswap 生态的“实验层”，方便后续更多 hooks 通过它被测试和推广；

4、竞争优势：未被 allowlist 的 hooks 在官方路由中处于劣势，Hookr 的池子在实际交易体验上更接近原生 Uniswap 池；

简而言之，这个路由层面的准入，对Hookr平台的交易量、用户体验和项目在 Uniswap 生态中的落地非常关键。

上推整整1年，一觉醒来4w粉了！

曾经的大号也神奇地找了回来，人生还是要向前看。

走到这个阶段，我已经不太关注粉丝的增长了。
真正的高质量，是诚实同步自己的成长。随着我探索得越来越深，内容必然走向硬核和深入，而刚入门的用户渐渐就看不懂了。

这意味着我可能会失去大众流量的增长机会，但比起为了数据迎合浅层需求，我更享受走向深水区。

回顾这1年，有几点深刻感悟：
1. 商单是甜蜜的毒药
连续两个月商单破10w，反而让我痛苦。既要对甲方负责，又要对读者真诚，极耗心力。最可怕的是，它剥夺了我原本玩AI的时间。我深知不能沉迷于这种线性收入，必须要平衡。

2. 现金流换取“Token 自由”，回归玩AI的纯粹快乐
越来越坚信，本地化部署是绝对的方向。赚到的钱，我全部砸向了硬件：买了4090机器、双卡V100，最近准备再上一台4卡机器。

买卡就为了一个目的：实现彻底的 Token 自由。
不用去管 API 账单和限频，让我能没有任何心理负担地探知未知领域、补充知识盲区、快乐地玩 AI；顺着自己的兴趣，静下心去磨出自己真正想做、且足够稳定的产品。

当拥有了算力自由，很多以前不敢想的事就自然发生了：自己做模型推理框架、做多卡权重分层调优，甚至做出了让自己沉迷一整天的游戏等等
这种在未知世界里探索的纯粹快乐，远胜于接单赚钱。

3. 赚钱从来不靠勤奋，靠的是选择与等待
推特上到处是一年赚几百万的声音，但在时代大潮面前，这些都不算大钱。
大多数人一辈子的财富，都是在极其短暂的2~3年内爆发出来的。而在此之前，你唯一要做的是在这个浪潮里扎根、沉淀心智、积蓄全部力量。

4.未来最赚钱的事，一定是AI做不了的事。
AI能做的事都可以换算成tokens

只要在自己热爱的领域里沉淀够深，当属于你的那个非线性机会到来时，你自然有能力毫不犹豫地全力押注。
